#1953. Newcastle United Women will have one hand on Title and Super League if winning this Sunderland derby

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

A huge match for Newcastle United Women and Tanya Oxtoby as they prepare for this Sunderland derby.

The Stadium of Light hosting at 2pm on Sunday 15 November.

After seven rounds of league matches Newcastle United Women are unbeaten and top of the second tier on 19 points from a possible 21, three clear of Sunderland.

It might seem a little premature when this derby clash is only the eighth match of the league season BUT a win for Newcastle United Women and they will surely already have one hand on the Title AND most importantly, promotion to the Super League.

It is only a 22 match season in the second tier and a win for Newcastle United Women would see them go six points clear of Sunderland with only 14 rounds of matches remaining, plus a minimum of at least five points clear of any other team, potentially more depending on how other results go on Sunday.

Only top spot guarantees automatic promotion to the Super League, as the teams that finish second and third in Women’s Super League 2 will play off for the right to face the team that finishes second bottom of WSL1 and a chance at promotion.

Tanya Oxtoby is manager of Newcastle United Women and has been talking ahead of facing Sunderland.

First of all, Tanya Oxtoby reflecting on last weekend’s 3-0 victory over Burnley at St James’ Park: “I really enjoyed watching it back. There were a lot of patterns of play and things we’ve been going after that were executed really well and consistently. There are, of course, still some bits to get better at, no doubt about that, but I was really pleased. To walk out at St. James’ Park and see that banner, Tanya Oxtoby’s Black and White Army, was just a real pinch me moment.”

Tanya Oxtoby on Newcastle United Women facing Sunderland: “Two teams in really good form with really good squads. It’s a great challenge for us and that’s what we’ve been talking about; the fact that we want to be pushed and we want to see how good we can be. We should embrace moments like this because it’s a positive thing.”

Tanya Oxtoby on what she wants from her players: “We talk a lot about making sure we’re proactive, and that we’re not being reactive to a certain game or a certain instant. We want to make sure that we’ve got our tools in the toolbox to be able to deal with that, and we’ve been working on that from pre-season, all the way through to now. We are who we are, and we want to go out and play our style of football, but it will be against a really good side. We’re going to have to think outside of the box in terms of solving problems when they appear.”

Tanya Oxtoby on the NUFC supporters: “They’re the best and you saw that on the weekend. We have the best fans and I know that they will come out in their numbers. I know that they will bring their voices. For us, our responsibility in that is to make sure that we put on a good performance they can be proud of, like we did last weekend.”

Best of luck to the lasses when they play against the Mackems on Sunday.

#1952. Max Dowman breaks Jude Bellingham record as Arsenal teenager makes England history

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Max Dowman has added another incredible achievement to his burgeoning career after becoming the youngest player to play for the England Under-21s.

The Arsenal youngster was introduced from the bench in Friday’s 1-0 friendly loss to Portugal at Ashton Gate. The 16-year-10-month-13-day-old player is over three months younger than Jude Bellingham was when he played his first game for the Under-21s.

Dowman replaced former Arsenal academy player Amario Cozier-Duberry in the 61st minute. He came on alongside debutant Trey Nyoni as England tried to shift the momentum of a challenging game.

An early strike from Afonso Moreira gave Portugal the lead in the 28th minute. An ineffective England team failed to respond. However, the replacements gave Lee Carsley’s team some late momentum.

Despite the hosts’ attempts to level the score, they failed to break down the Portuguese defence. The result means England have lost for the second game running. However, Dowman had much to be pleased with personally.

Dowman has added to his growing collection of records.

He became the youngest player to play in the Champions League, the youngest goalscorer in the history of the Premier League and the youngest to win the Premier League title.

Breaking Bellingham’s England Under-21 record is another significant step. It shows how quickly Dowman has progressed through the international age groups.

He has already made a big impression at Arsenal with Mikel Arteta’s love of giving younger players a chance, but Dowman will have some stiff competition for first team minutes.

Another positive is his progression on an international scale. He will improve both physically and tactically playing against older players and gain experience at a higher level.

England will host France in their next friendly on Monday, 16th November. Dowman will be hoping to feature after his instant impact on the record books.

Despite the disappointing result against Portugal, it was a landmark evening for the Arsenal players.

Dowman is already building a legacy at club level, but now he can add to his list of records by becoming an England Under-21 record holder.

At just 16, he has plenty of time to improve and show consistent performances to get more opportunities with the senior Arsenal squad.

#1951. West Ham’s Interest In Sydie Peck Resurfaces After Summer Pursuit

West Ham United have once again been linked with Sheffield United midfielder Sydie Peck, with transfer journalist Ekrem Konur reporting that the Hammers are continuing to scout the 22-year-old.

The England Under-21 international has attracted attention from several clubs, with Newcastle United and Sunderland also named in the report. Peck has certainly done his reputation no harm recently, scoring a hat-trick against Preston North End earlier this month, although there is no suggestion that West Ham have made a formal approach.

Interestingly, this isn’t the first time Peck has been linked with a move to the London Stadium. ExWHUEmployee reported through The West Ham Way back in July that West Ham had been monitoring the midfielder even before the arrival of director of recruitment Nils Koppen.

I looked quite closely at Peck during the summer when West Ham were first linked with him, and I have to say, he was a player who caught the attention.

Back then, however, we didn’t know who was staying and who was going, and the midfield situation was very different.

Since then, West Ham have signed Arne Engels and retained Soungoutou Magassa, while Mohamadou Kanté has emerged as one of the most encouraging performers of the season.

I think Peck is a decent player. Very good, in fact, and somebody who would be extremely useful in the Championship.

But unless there are due to be significant outgoings, I just cannot see this one happening.

Kante has become an important player for West Ham

Lewis Orford is not getting enough game time as it is, and Mohamadou Kanté is having one hell of a breakout season. I wouldn’t particularly want to bring anybody in who might stop that.

And let’s not forget the point Nils Koppen has made about West Ham’s recruitment strategy: the club don’t want to sign players who block the pathway of youngsters coming through.

It’s a philosophy I agree with, particularly when we’ve got young players already showing that they deserve opportunities.

There is clearly something about Peck that West Ham’s recruitment department likes. After all, the interest was being reported before Koppen arrived, and his performances for Sheffield United have only strengthened his case.

But there’s a difference between identifying a good player and identifying a player you actually need.

West Ham have more pressing areas of the squad to strengthen, and unless Scott Parker is expecting a major shake-up in midfield, I’d be surprised to see the club pursue this particular deal in January.

#1950. Xabi Alonso was brought in to end the chaos at Chelsea and he is failing. PLUS: Football's most vanilla pundit gives out-of-his-depth Michael Carrick an easy ride: IAN LADYMAN on My Football Weekend

Published: 07:00 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 07:55 EST, 9 November 2026

The whiff of Premier League failure is in the air as the smoke clears from Bonfire Night.

It always feels this way by the time we get to the November international break.

Managers and their players have had time to settle in and teething problems no longer cut it as a reason for autumn struggles.

Worst of all, Christmas is coming and we all know what tends to happen to teams who are struggling as the end of the year nears.

So at places like Manchester United, Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Newcastle and Spurs there is anxiety about expectations not being met.

Xabi Alonso was hired to break the cycle at Chelsea and he is not yet succeeding

Xabi Alonso's side would appear to be the team that is failing without anybody seeming to notice.

At Stamford Bridge, the environment is conducive to Alonso and his team doing well this season.

Chelsea – not in Europe after last season's troubles – are only playing once a week. So Alonso – hired for his coaching reputation – has time on the grass with players who should arrive every weekend with freshness in their legs.

It's the environment that enabled Michael Carrick to fool everyone at Manchester United last season. While the rest of the Premier League got bogged down in the schedule, United sailed upwards on the back of a lighter load.

When we look at Alonso's team we see only familiar Chelsea things – and not in a good way.

Inconsistent tactics, some strange selections and, on the back of it, some very ordinary results.

This is the cycle Alonso was hired to break and he is not yet succeeding.

Sunday's defeat to Sunderland can be added to league setbacks against Spurs, Brentford and Arsenal.

They were unimpressive in beating United a couple of weeks ago also. Carrick's team outplayed them in the first half and should have been two or three goals ahead.

Under Alonso, Chelsea are yet to establish an identity or discernible patterns. It is hard to know yet what his best back four (or five) looks like. In the absence of the injured striker Joao Pedro, Alonso seems happier to play without one rather than use Danny Welbeck, signed for just this scenario in the summer.

The absence of Joao Pedro is significant while Alonso is also without his first choice goalkeeper Emi Martinez. These things matter.

But Chelsea have a huge squad of international players. Maybe it's too big. Whatever the case Alonso must get the best out of it soon.

Nobody seems to be talking about how very underwhelming the whole thing feels. But if it continues, they soon will be.

On Match of the Day on Sunday night, football's most vanilla pundit Dion Dublin was asked whether Michael Carrick has done enough to keep his job.

'I think so,' said Dublin. 'I think Michael has all the tools but the players just aren't doing what they need to do.'

At every other club in the Premier League, under-performing players and the bad results that tend to follow lead to intense scrutiny and criticism of the manager. It's his job to affect these things.

Not at United, though, where the level of public and media support for Carrick remains extraordinary and illogical.

If we applied this level of leeway to everybody else then nobody would ever be sacked.

Dion Dublin, pictured on Homes Under The Hammer duty, gave Michael Carrick an easy ride

Carrick is out of his depth at sinking Manchester United - his team are a shambles

Yes, there are a number of factors at play at Old Trafford. Yes, we know what they are and who is to blame for them. Yes, it's a very difficult job.

But the truth is that Carrick is failing in a quite spectacular fashion.

Of all the managers to have followed Sir Alex Ferguson over the last 13 and a half years, Erik ten Hag was the one who looked most out of his depth in terms of the chaotic nature of his team's football.

Carrick is now on the way to eclipsing that. His team are a shambles and that's on him. Once again, this is a mediocre league and it's quite criminal that Carrick has his group of players in the bottom three.

The former Middlesbrough manager is so out of his depth it's quite painful to watch.

It was another extraordinary afternoon at Old Trafford as United drew 4-4 with Aston Villa.

Unai Emery's Villa team is going through yet another regeneration after the sale of big-name players in the summer and balancing the Champions League with domestic football will once again be a challenge.

Emery seems to have made his mind up about one of his squad members, though, after former United and Chelsea winger Alejandro Garnacho was left out of the squad entirely yesterday.

Garnacho is a talented player but has made only 14 Premier League starts – and none at Villa – since leaving Old Trafford for Chelsea in the summer of 2025.

The Argentine is still only 22 so time is on his side but at some point he is going to have to do something on the field to justify the investment in a career that is currently going nowhere.

Alejandro Garnacho was left out of the squad entirely yesterday by Aston Villa

Sky's excellent touchline reporter Patrick Davison had his work cut out post-match at Old Trafford as he interviewed one manager in danger of the sack and another who had just flounced down the tunnel like a chap with his pants on fire.

Neither Michael Carrick nor Unai Emery seemed particularly comfortable in the face of Davison's questions and that's exactly as it should be.

He is there to ask questions on behalf of a broadcaster that ploughs billions of pounds into our national sport each year. He is not there to apply soothing balm.

There would appear to be many others happy to do that anyway.

Sky's Patrick Davison (right) is not there to apply soothing balm with his questions

Less impressive was the appearance of Sky's latest metric that appeared on screen during Nottingham Forest's dismantling of Manchester City on Saturday.

Titled simply 'pressures' it indicated that Forest were doing rather better at it than City.

But what did it mean? Does anybody know? Or indeed care?

Two seasons ago at the City Ground I saw local boy Ryan Yates give Casemiro such a chasing as Forest beat Manchester United that the great Brazilian was taken off before he was sent off.

On Saturday by the river, Yates made his first league start of the season as Oliver Glasner’s team overwhelmed City.

Beforehand Yates gave an address to his team-mates. He told them about what it meant to play for the club and touched briefly on its history.

He told me once in an interview that he tends to tell all new arrivals at Forest what the two stars on the shirt actually mean – two European Cups won in 1979 and 1980.

It’s smart work by a lad who knows what football means in Nottingham and it was smart work by his manager who knew that his team needed an injection of something visceral to drag him from a trough of failure that was threatening to cost him his job.

Manchester United could probably do with a bit of that right now. So, possibly, could Chelsea and indeed Tottenham. At Liverpool, they lament the absence from the team of Trent Alexander-Arnold and Curtis Jones.

It takes an awful lot to make up a Premier League team these days. Place of birth is not a priority any more and that’s understandable. But sometimes it helps.

When was the last time an English team won the title with a poor goalkeeper?

Flick back over the last couple of decades and it's hard to find an example.

So what hope for Manchester City this season?

Gianluigi Donnarumma is anything but a poor goalkeeper but the problem is that he is playing like one and it is there that City's current problems start.

Enzo Maresca's back four looks shot to pieces and that often happens when they lose faith in the chap behind them.

Maresca says he won't change. 'My team is Gigi plus ten others,' is his take.

Enzo Maresca says he will not change goalkeeper despite Gianluigi Donnarumma's problems

His back up is 34-year-old Argentinean Geronimo Rulli, a member of his country's World Cup squad with nine caps to his name.

Rulli is well-travelled and has some pedigree. He was, for example, Villarreal's hero as they beat Manchester United in a Europa League final shoot out in 2021.

If Maresca trusts him then maybe now is the time to show it. If he doesn't then why did City sign him?

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson is perhaps not quite what he once was at the age of 34 but produced a throwback performance for his team at Crystal Palace. Without him, Liverpool would not have won.

Nevertheless Palace's struggles go on and their coach Pierre Sage is in danger of losing his job.

However the south London club cannot say they were not warned about trouble ahead.

Former manager Oliver Glasner spent most of last season in a huff about what he saw as a failure by the Palace board to invest properly in the squad.

Palace have won twice in ten Premier League games this season and it seems Glasner may have been right.

Brighton continue to fly high and to produce such an energetic performance to beat Brentford having played away at Getafe in Europe on Thursday was testimony to the fitness of Fabian Hurzeler's squad.

The Seagulls were certainly helped by having to play against ten for an hour, though, and on Match of the Day the enduringly listenable Jonathan Pearce spoke for all of us as he watched Chema Andres go down after minimal contact to his cheek from Brentford's Igor Thiago.

'That was nothing, nothing, nothing,' said Pearce as Thiago walked off.

Coming so soon after theatrics from Alexis MacAllister and Gabriel in the Liverpool-Arsenal game last week, the issue of players exaggerating facial contact to get opponents sent off remains a live one.

Brentford's manager Keith Andrews was measured on the issue but suggested the tactic was becoming 'a game within a game'.

It's a problem and referees head Howard Webb needs his officials to get a grip of it.

Brighton's Pascal Gross has now created more than 25 chances for team-mates this season and that's more than anyone else in the Premier League.

Gross cost £1.2million when he returned to the club from Borussia Dortmund last January.

It constitutes another steal in the market by Brighton's stat boffins but this time they probably didn't need the data to convince them of its merits.

Pascal Gross scored on Sunday and has now created more than 25 chances for team-mates

Bournemouth, meanwhile, cast their net as widely as anybody these days and that includes all the way down the English pyramid.

The South Coast club – on an eight-match winning streak now under Marco Rose – have a relationship with yesterday's FA Cup giant killers Wimborne from the seventh tier.

Wimborne of the Southern League Premier South beat League Two Crawley in Round One and will this week send their Chilean teenage striker Angel Diaz for a trial at the Premier League club.

Story of last season in the EFL was probably Lincoln City's promotion to the Championship where, after 15 games, they are just about keeping their heads above water in 21st place.

Architect of that incredible rise was former futsal coach Michael Skubala who rather sullied the romantic feel of it all by quitting almost immediately to join Bristol City.

This weekend Skubala's team were thrashed 5-0 at home by Norwich with the home fans singing that their manager would be 'sacked in the morning'.

Lincoln have already won at Ashton Gate, back in September, at the start of a run that has seen City win just two from ten.

Sometimes, it really does pay just to stay where you are.

#1949. Ten things I hate about football (Part Two)

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Having put the boot into pitch-soaking preliminaries, flamethrowers, silly kick-offs, unpunished obstruction and ball-playing keepers in my previous article, I felt some of my frustrations with the modern game starting to dissipate. Not for long, though, as I raged against five other deeply annoying aspects of football today.

The continual expansion of non-domestic tournaments is a right pain.

Not only do the overblown Champions League and other Uefa-run competitions last far too long, they cause severe collateral damage to such venerable institutions as the FA Cup (1872) and what was the Football League (1888) until television moved the goalposts in 1992.

Where Uefa goes, of course, its equally power-hungry brothers in Fifa are bound to follow, with the money-making exercises known as the Club World Championship and the World Cup. As one friend, a football agnostic, said when invited to watch yet another match from last summer’s tournament: “I’m living in a world of pain.” Sorry, Walter. Gianni Infantino’s questionable leadership of both organisations has feathered a lot of nests while running the risk of killing the goose that lays the golden eggs.

Who didn’t love FA Cup replays? One of my fondest memories is the second replay of the Newcastle v Bolton fifth-round cup tie in the 1975-76 season. After drawn games home and away, the third match was played on neutral territory. The brainboxes at Lancaster Gate in London, which was FA HQ until 2000, presumably looked at a map of northern England and decided Elland Road was a fitting venue.

In those days, the words “neutral” and “Leeds” were seen in the same sentence as often as childcare and King Herod. After United finally vanquished the Wanderers, the brick-wielding West Yorkshire hoolies ambushed us on the way back to the railway station. Happy to say we also won that encounter . . .

Replays have been scrapped by degrees; from the fifth round onwards in 2019-20, then completely from 2024-25. Teams playing in Uefa competitions are given a pass to the third round of the League Cup and the “smaller” clubs who are essential to the health of football have been thoroughly shafted.

The chance of a money-spinning tie in front of 60,000-plus spectators has been greatly reduced, allegedly to ease fixture congestion. No longer can fans relish the vendettas that were often triggered by replayed ties.

Such occasions have been usurped by knockout competitions that reach the exciting bit only after a whole host of tedious league-phase matches. If that’s progress, you can stick it where the sun doesn’t shine.

Once television paid the piper, it was bound to call the tune. The Premier League is one of many competitions beholden to the billions of pounds offered for worldwide broadcasting rights. If Sky or TNT doesn’t want a match to start at 3pm on Saturday, the time will be altered. Supporters travelling almost the length of England are treated with contempt. This trend has spread like a plague from the top tier to all the lower divisions.

You might have a 700-mile round trip to the Amex or the Vitality but be a good chap, set off at midday on a Friday or a Monday for an 8pm kick-off. Book a post-match hotel while you’re at it. Because the last train home left before the match started. The atmosphere you generate is an essential element of the viewers’ experience, of course. To show how much your enthusiastic support is appreciated, we’ll charge only £30 a ticket. Just remember to be grateful . .

While TV has done spectators no favours, neither has it considered the sensibilities of referees. They had it relatively easy in the days when only the FA Cup final and the League Cup final were broadcast live. Yes, I doubt the man in black enjoyed hearing his parentage mocked by 50,000 screaming fans but he could just laugh it off.

Trial by television has now taken centre stage. With countless replays of debatable incidents in super slo-mo, there is no hiding place. Rentagob former players, who in their prime would have cheated without compunction to gain an advantage, queue up to find fault. They might not know the laws of the game but that won’t stop them grinding their axe.

I like goal-line technology. I hate marginal offside calls, when the judgment is based on which particular freeze-frame the jokers at Stockley Park decide to use.

Many decisions made by the man (or woman) in the middle are debatable. That doesn’t necessarily mean they are wrong. Though if Jarred Gillett is involved, they usually are.

One particular bit of foul play makes my blood boil. It is sneaky, cowardly and reckless. It is also rarely punished, because most referees seem unable to see what’s occurring.

We all know the scenario: an aerial pass is contested by two or more players. It is perhaps nine feet above the pitch. One player leaps for the ball, eyes fixed on it. Let’s call him Big Dan Burn, for instance. The other doesn’t fancy his chances of winning possession fairly. Let’s call him Kai Havertz . . .

Herr Havertz looks briefly at the ball, then assesses when Burn will jump. The German nudges, pushes or backs into the Colossus from Blyth while he is in mid-air. Down he crashes, in an uncontrolled descent dictated by the laws of physics.

The referee almost always sees nothing wrong. No free kick, no card, let the game flow . . . In one such incident Burn fractured a few bones in his back. After the final whistle, the detestable Arsenal manager ranted and raved because Anthony Gordon’s winning goal had not been disallowed. If only the lickspittle interviewer had mimicked Del Boy talking to Rodney and said: “Shut up, you tart!”

They say money talks. That’s certainly true in football, though Dylan was more accurate when he sang “money doesn’t talk, it swears” on It’s Alright, Ma (I’m Only Bleeding).

For as long as I can recall, the overwhelming trend has been: to the richest, the glory. In the 1960s Manchester United were financially bolstered by Louis Edwards, whose company supplied meat products of interesting quality to thousands of schools.

In the 70s Liverpool reaped the dividends of long-term investment by the Moores family, whose fortunes came from football pools and retailing. The Moores also had a stake in Everton, a big force in the 80s.

In the 90s Jack Walker, a Blackburn businessman, paid for a team to win the newish Premier League. Ten years later Roman Abramovich, a fine and upstanding Russian oligarch, rescued Chelsea from financial oblivion. He was forced to relinquish control after his pal Putin ordered troops to invade Ukraine.

Arsenal got into bed with Alisher Usmanov, another man who had made billions after the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was the club’s biggest shareholder by 2009. As a Gunner told me on the train up to London this month for the Fulham v NUFC game: “Thank goodness he left before the doo-doo hit the fan.”

Meanwhile, Abu Dhabi money was about to transform Manchester City from also-rans into the pre-eminent force in English football.

Newcastle United’s current owners almost certainly wanted to do the same when they bought the club five years ago. They have not been allowed that freedom, so far, though they have twice overseen Champions League qualification for the first time in a generation and the first Wembley cup final win since 1955.

Football is no longer sport in the true sense. The playing field has never been less level, the vested interests never more entrenched. The Premier League, Uefa and Fifa are all complicit in this lucrative merry-go-round.

Apologies for donning my rose-tinted spectacles . . . but some things were better in the good old days.

#1948. Martin Ødegaard sends clear message to Arsenal amid Bayern Munich transfer rumours

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Martin Ødegaard has spoken out about the speculation surrounding his future. He has stated he would like to stay at Arsenal for the future.

The captain has also admitted that talks about a new deal have not yet begun. Ødegaard is currently under contract until the summer of 2028. This leaves Arsenal with an important decision to make over the coming months.

Bayern Munich are being linked with an interest in the midfielder according to reports from Germany. The Bundesliga giants are said to be keeping their eyes on the player’s situation.

Speaking while on international duty with Norway, Ødegaard was quick to dismiss the speculation. He made it clear he is settled in north London and sees his future being at the Emirates Stadium.

There is no suggestion that the 27-year-old is seeking a move. Although comments do highlight a contract issue that Arsenal will be keen to resolve in the short term.

The Norwegian’s laid-back attitude should be encouraging for supporters.

He has made it clear that he is happy at the club and wants to stay here for the time being. This means that there is no need to panic.

However, Arsenal will have to get him to sign on the dotted line. Leaving his captain in the last year of his contract with no progress would cause an unnecessary distraction.

Since his permanent move from Real Madrid in 2021, Ødegaard has become a key player in Mikel Arteta’s plans. He has grown into a team leader and is one of the most influential players in the dressing room.

His importance has been shown by his inclusion in all 10 of Arsenal’s Premier League games so far this season. He has scored three goals.

This is a big improvement on last season, where he was hampered by injuries and failed to make much of an impact in front of goal.

It wouldn’t be a shock to see Bayern Munich show interest in Ødegaard, but don’t take this as a sign he is close to a move.

There is little reason for Arsenal to consider losing their captain. He brings so much more to the team than just his technical ability and has been relied upon by Arteta to lead by example.

The midfielder was also pivotal in the 1-0 win over Hull City on 7 November, scoring the winner in the 72nd minute to give the league leaders three crucial points.

Arsenal have put themselves in a good position in the title race. Keeping their key players happy will be important in the second half of the campaign.

The Gunners will be focused on their game against Newcastle United on 21st November.

Arsenal fans have no real reason to panic at the moment, with the captain wanting to stay at the club and his comments suggesting he is happy.

However, it would be a good idea for the club to try and ensure his long-term future at the club. Ødegaard is still an important part of Arteta’s strategy, and ensuring he stays at the club would be a smart move.

#1947. West Ham’s Former Celtic Starlet Gets Chance To Prove Himself

West Ham United striker Daniel Cummings is reportedly set to join National League side Aldershot Town on loan, according to transfer journalist Pete O’Rourke. The move has yet to be officially confirmed, but it would give the 20-year-old his first sustained opportunity to prove himself in senior football.

Interestingly, Cummings would be joining a club he scored against earlier this season. The young Scot was on target when West Ham’s Under-21s beat Aldershot 3-0 in the National League Cup back in September, so at least his prospective new employers have already had a decent look at him.

Much was made of West Ham signing Cummings from Celtic in the summer of 2025. The talented forward had been scoring goals for fun in the Bhoys’ academy set-up and had even been handed a Champions League appearance by Brendan Rodgers. In many respects, it seemed as though the youngster had the world at his feet.

Rodgers was understandably miffed that Cummings refused to sign a new deal at Celtic Park. Mark Noble, meanwhile, had spotted a potential bargain, and West Ham moved to secure the young forward for a compensation fee reportedly below £500,000.

Unfortunately, things haven’t quite worked out as hoped.

The breakthrough into West Ham’s first team has never materialised, and although Cummings has scored goals for the development squad, he hasn’t dominated at that level in quite the way many might have expected.

Rodgers was disappointed Cummings didn’t sign a Celtic deal

To be fair to him, his progress was disrupted by a shoulder injury shortly after joining the Hammers. He has subsequently returned to goalscoring form, including a brace against Braintree Town last month.

Nevertheless, he still looks a long way from establishing himself in the West Ham first team.

The move would at least give Cummings the opportunity to play regular senior football, something he has previously spoken about wanting.

Of course, there’s a significant difference between scoring goals in academy football and doing so against experienced professionals in the National League. Whether Aldershot is the ideal level for him remains to be seen, but it’s an opportunity to demonstrate what he can do.

Aldershot isn’t a million miles away from me, so maybe I’ll pop over and have a look at him myself.

I certainly wish him well and genuinely hope this could be the making of him as a footballer. Clearly there’s talent there, otherwise he wouldn’t have attracted so much attention at Celtic.

Hopefully, regular first-team football is exactly what he needs to start fulfilling that early promise.

#1944. ‘If I stayed…’ – Rio Ngumoha reflects on ‘no-brainer’ decision to swap Chelsea for Liverpool

Rio Ngumoha has said that his decision to swap Chelsea for Liverpool in 2024 was a ‘no-brainer’.

The Reds signed the teenage winger from the London club’s academy just after he turned 16, with a subsequent tribunal determining that the Merseysiders were to pay an initial £2.8m (potentially rising to £6.8m) in compensation.

The now 18-year-old has gone on to make 44 appearances and counting for LFC’s first team, along with winning three senior England caps, and he’s turned in some man-of-the-match performances at Champions League level.

In a recent media interview (via The Standard), Ngumoha explained that he decided to leave Chelsea for Liverpool because he saw a clearer pathway to the first team at Anfield than he did in west London.

The winger said: “I needed a new challenge. I feel like if I stayed at Chelsea… not saying I wouldn’t have got to the first team as quickly, because I believe in my ability, but I feel Liverpool just gave me a new pathway.

“The plan they set for me was straightforward. For me, it was a no-brainer going to Liverpool.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The Reds have had a fine track record for attracting top-class teenage talents in recent years, and Ngumoha is perhaps the standout signing in that category.

That Liverpool were prepared to go through a rigorous registration process with the Premier League (as the winger was a minor at the time) shows just how determined they were to see the deal through, and all of that bureaucratic effort has proven to be more than worth it.

In little more than a year, the teenager has gone from highly-rated prospect to established first-team presence, and there’s a palpable excitement among the fans at Anfield every time he gets the ball, with many a defender bamboozled by his phenomenal dribbling ability and supreme self-confidence.

Ngumoha’s leap of faith in joining the Reds has been vindicated by his regularity of senior football, especially this season as he’s started almost half of our matches across all competitions, and full credit to him for seizing his opportunity when it’s been handed to him.

Chelsea’s loss has very much proven to be our gain, and with the 18-year-old now holding a market value of €50m (£41.8m), that aforementioned compensation fee looks increasingly like one of the steals of the century.

#1942. Why West Ham’s Fulham Defeat Gives Scott Parker Plenty To Be Pleased About

West Ham United were beaten 1-0 by Fulham in a behind-closed-doors friendly on Thursday, but I don’t think the result matters at all. If anything, losing by just one goal to Premier League opposition when we’ve got ten players missing on international duty is no shame whatsoever.

According to ExWHUEmployee, reporting through The West Ham Way, the match was arranged to give Scott Parker an opportunity to assess some of his players and help others build up their match fitness. No team sheet has been made public, so we don’t know exactly who featured.

What I’m particularly impressed by is how quickly Parker has organised and sorted this out. He’s barely been in the job five minutes, yet he’s already managed to arrange a friendly against Premier League opposition, presumably using his Fulham connections to get it done. That’s exactly the sort of proactive approach needed to drag the club back up the league table.

The bit I found particularly interesting was the emphasis on getting players up to fitness.

From that point of view, I’d have thought Soungoutou Magassa and Edson Álvarez would be prime candidates to have participated in the game. Alphonse Areola would also be an obvious beneficiary if he’s recovered sufficiently from his recent injury.

It’s also important for Parker to have a look at some of the other academy goalkeepers, particularly given the concerns over Fin Herrick’s fitness and the recent poor form of Mads Hermansen.

I’d rather hope Lewis Orford played some part in the game as well. He’s not getting nearly enough first-team football, and this would have been an ideal opportunity to show the new manager what he can do.

And, as I wrote earlier this week, the international break is going to afford Pablo the opportunity to try to impress the new Hammers manager.

Parker omitted the Brazilian striker from his first two matchday squads altogether, so a friendly like this could have been particularly useful for him.

We already knew that Parker’s preparations would be disrupted by the international call-ups, but he’s clearly not prepared to sit around waiting for everybody to return.

He’s taken a situation where ten players are unavailable and turned it into an opportunity to assess the rest of his squad against decent opposition.

I wouldn’t be remotely concerned about the 1-0 defeat. We don’t know who played, how many substitutions were made or even whether Parker was particularly interested in winning the match. Hopefully those details will be revealed by Ex later today?

For all we know, he may have learnt more from this game than he would have from a comfortable victory against weaker opposition.

It’s a thumbs up from me for Parker being proactive, particularly so early in his West Ham managerial career.

The only question is whether he’ll arrange another friendly next week before the Championship resumes against Preston.

#1941. West Ham-Linked Rangers Giant Features In Spain Victory

West Ham United transfer target Ryan Naderi was handed a starting place for Czechia against Spain in Thursday night’s UEFA Nations League encounter, which ended in a 2-0 victory for the Spanish.

The 6ft 4in Rangers striker, who has recently been linked with a January move to West Ham, played 66 minutes before being substituted. Spain took the lead through an Álex Baena penalty in the 39th minute, with Marc Pubill adding a second deep into stoppage time.

There was another West Ham connection to the match, with Tomáš Souček returning to international action as an 85th-minute substitute as Marin covered earlier today. Former Hammers Vladimír Coufal and Alex Král were also in the Czech starting line-up.

As Claret & Hugh reported yesterday, West Ham have been linked with Naderi following his impressive start to life at Rangers.

The 23-year-old has reportedly attracted interest from several clubs, although Rangers are understood to be reluctant to sell their striker during the January transfer window. Spain’s victory leaves them with five wins from five Nations League fixtures.

That sets up a particularly interesting encounter with England at the Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid on Sunday evening. The three lions spluttered to a 2-1 victory against Slaven Bilic’s Croatia last with Harry Kane scoring the winner from the spot.

The two sides are competing for top spot in Group A3, with the match kicking off at 7.45pm GMT.

Meanwhile, from a West Ham perspective, it is encouraging to see Souček back on the pitch following his recent injury problems, even if his involvement was limited to the closing stages.

#1939. ‘Unlikely to be…’ – Journalist sounds contract renewal warning over Van Dijk and Alisson

Liverpool fans have been advised that prospective contract renewals for Virgil van Dijk and Alisson Becker could take time to materialise.

The future of both long-serving players has been in the spotlight this week after they publicly addressed their respective situations, with the goalkeeper’s agent already in talks with club chiefs while the captain has maintained a more neutral ‘let’s see’ stance.

Their current deals are set to expire next June, and they’ll be able to sign pre-contract agreements with overseas clubs from the beginning of January unless they extend their terms with the Reds before then.

In an article for The Athletic discussing the futures of Van Dijk and Alisson, James Pearce warned that ‘there is unlikely to be a quick resolution’ to either player’s contract situation, citing how renewals for the Dutchman and Mo Salah two seasons ago weren’t confirmed until April 2025.

The journalist explained how Liverpool would need to take a pragmatic approach to the renewal process and not be led by sentiment, with the defender turning 36 next July and the goalkeeper’s 35th birthday coming three months later.

In a more hopeful note, Pearce wrote: ‘It makes sense for all parties to wait and see how things unfold in the coming weeks and months. Respect abounds and relationships are strong, with dialogue ongoing between sporting director Julian Ward and the pair’s camps.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

The case studies of Van Dijk and Salah from 2024/25 indicate that we ought not to expect a swift resolution to the current contract situations regarding the Dutchman and Alisson, with negotiations set to involve substantial back-and-forth before any agreement is struck.

Considering ther importance on the pitch, they’re two of the highest-earning players in the current Liverpool squad, with the captain leading the way on £350,000 per week and the goalkeeper pocketing a weekly wage of £250,000 (Capology).

For their deals to be renewed, it’d either take a significant deflection from club policy to hand out lucrative extensions to players in their mid-30s, or the pair to accept a reduction on their base salary and increase the value of performance-related bonuses on offer.

In truth, the contract negotiations for Van Dijk and Alisson will likely run for another few months, and there could be some frayed nerves among Kopites if either or both situations were still unresolved by spring.

However, with the duo proving this season that they remain top-class performers bringing some crucial stability to a much-changed team, Ward must make every effort to keep them at Anfield for at least another year, and we’re cautiously optimistic that both will remain Reds players going into the 2027/28 campaign.

#1938. West Ham Ticket Row: A Bit Of Pettiness? I’m All For It

West Ham United’s ticketing arrangements for the forthcoming Championship clash with Bristol City have caused controversy, but I have to say I’m firmly on the Hammers’ side with this one. If there’s an element of tit for tat involved, I don’t have a problem with it at all.

Bristol City supporters might not particularly like the situation, but there is some history between the two clubs when it comes to ticket allocations. During the FA Cup meeting in January 2024, Bristol City took their full allocation of around 9,000 tickets at the London Stadium, resulting in thousands of West Ham season-ticket holders having to move from their usual seats.

That caused considerable frustration at the time, with the West Ham United Supporters’ Trust seeking clarification from the club over the arrangements. So if the current situation feels like a bit of payback, I can certainly understand why.

One thing West Ham’s relegation to the Championship has provided is a real reality check when it comes to the treatment of travelling supporters.

In the Premier League, there was at least some collective understanding that away supporters shouldn’t be completely fleeced. The Football Supporters’ Federation’s original Twenty’s Plenty campaign eventually helped bring about the £30 away-ticket cap, which has remained in place since 2016.

It wasn’t perfect, and £30 was still more than supporters had originally campaigned for, but at least there was a limit.

That protection doesn’t exist across the Championship, and we’re now seeing the difference.

Take West Ham’s trip to Birmingham City in December, for example. According to the club’s official ticket information, adult supporters will be charged £37.50 for the privilege of watching the Hammers at St Andrew’s.

And it definitely feels like Championship clubs are treating us like absolute mugs.

When West Ham roll into town, we’re seen as a cash cow. Clubs know we’re going to bring a substantial travelling support, and it increasingly feels as though they’re happy to make the most of it.

Of course, I understand that Championship clubs have their own financial pressures, but that doesn’t make it any easier for supporters who are already spending a fortune travelling around the country.

I don’t have a problem with West Ham looking after our own fans, even if that means upsetting a few visiting supporters along the way.

Perhaps there’s a little bit of pettiness involved, but realistically, I don’t mind that either.

We’re West Ham, and the club should be looking after our fans. That ought to be the priority, particularly when supporters have been asked to put up with so much since dropping into the Championship.

And any Bristol City fans who don’t like it probably should look at their own club’s conduct when we played them in the FA Cup.

I don’t particularly want to see football clubs getting into an endless argument over ticket allocations, and ultimately I’d prefer supporters everywhere to be treated fairly.

But when it comes to this particular situation, I’m not going to criticise the West Ham hierarchy for giving a bit back.

Sometimes tit for tat is exactly what it looks like, and on this occasion, I’m perfectly happy with it.

#1935. Declan Rice reveals he's stepped back from social media because it can 'ruin your whole day' after sick trolling of him and his girlfriend - as he poses in new photoshoot

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 06:36 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 08:45 EST, 9 November 2026

Declan Rice has opened up about reducing his use of social media - citing the mental toll it can have.

The Arsenal and England midfielder has been subjected to online abuse in the past - with his long-term partner Lauren Fryer having also been targeted.

Online abuse about her appearance had led to Fryer wiping all posts from her Instagram page back in 2024.

While Rice still has an Instagram account, he quit X three years ago as a result of the negativity that app can bring.

'I've not been back on the app since,' he told GQ Magazine - after being named among their Men of the Year. 'You could be having a great morning. You read one thing, and it just ruins your whole day.

'I feel like that's one of my strongest points... the ability to block out noise and not deal with that kind of stuff.'

Declan Rice has revealed he quit X three years ago due to the abuse he would receive online

Rice and long-term partner Lauren Fryer have been targeted in the past (pair pictured with their son Jude in May)

The midfielder says one post could 'ruin' his whole day - even if he was a great day beforehand

Rice, who has a four-year-old son called Jude with Fryer, is worried about the impact of social media on the younger generations.

'Screen time, for me, isn't a big thing,' he says of his own personal phone usage. 'I think social media for kids is 100 per cent a problem. I don't feel like there's as much personality now as there was a few years ago.'

As detailed by Daily Mail Sport last month, the 27-year-old is closing in on a new long-term deal at Arsenal believed to be worth around £350,000 per week.

The contract will put him on a level footing with Bukayo Saka at the top of the club's salary list.

And speaking about money in football as a whole, Rice told GQ Magazine that the finances within the sport are 'ridiculous' and despite his wealth he still wants to set a good example to his son Jude.

'The money that's in football as a whole is just ridiculous,' he continued. 'It's important to understand what things cost, even if you don't have to worry about paying for them.

'You still want to teach your kid values, not wanting them to be spoiled. You want them to work and to understand the value of life and money.

'It makes you more comfortable to be able to do things. But I don't wake up and think, "Oh, I've got loads of money", it's not the end goal.'

The 27-year-old is worried about the pitfalls of social media on the younger generations

The 27-year-old Arsenal and England star has been named in GQ Magazine's Men of the Year

Rice's focus will now be on his country with England hosting Croatia on Thursday night in the UEFA Nations League before travelling to World Cup champions Spain on Sunday.

Going into the November international break, the midfielder is enjoying a fine season with Arsenal who sit six points clear at the top of the Premier League with 27 points from their opening 10 matches.

#1934. “I don’t know why…” – John Aldridge fears Liverpool’s stance on one player could ‘backfire’

John Aldridge has questioned why Liverpool weren’t more assertive in pulling Dominik Szoboszlai out of national team duty when he’s currently nursing a minor injury.

The midfielder sprained his ankle in the 3-1 victory at Crystal Palace on Sunday, with Andoni Iraola uncertain after the game as to whether or not the 26-year-old would join up with his country during this international window.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Hungarian FA said that a decision on the player’s participation against Georgia and Northern Ireland over the next week will be deferred until the ‘last minute’ as his fitness continues to be assessed.

In his latest column for the Liverpool Echo, Aldridge voiced his belief that Liverpool should’ve done more to prevent Szoboszlai from playing for Hungary in the coming days when he’s clearly not fully fit.

The former Reds striker wrote: ‘I know Virgil van Dijk has pulled out of the Netherlands squad because of a little niggle, but Dominik Szoboszlai has stayed with Hungary despite injuring his knee against Palace.

‘Any other club would pull them out of international duty. Manchester United, Arsenal, Man City – they’d all pull them. We’ve seen it before. Any doubt and that’s it, decision made, you’re not playing. I don’t understand why we don’t throw our weight around like that.

‘I understand players want to play for their country. I was the same with Ireland. I would answer call-ups even when I was injured. I get what it means and how much it means to players, but any other club would just pull them. That’s not happened here, I don’t know why. Hopefully that just means it’s not that serious.

‘It still sounds like they’re taking a risk. If he stays with Hungary and plays, we’ve just got to hope the decision doesn’t backfire and come back to hurt Liverpool.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

As Szoboszlai is contracted to Liverpool, the Merseyside club could’ve blocked him from representing his country during this international window because of his knee injury.

However, it’d appear to be a case of the player wanting to at least link up with the Hungary camp and try to prove his fitness, and Anfield chiefs green-lighting that action out of respect for the 26-year-old and not wanting to antagonise him by forbidding him to travel.

The grey area over the midfielder potentially being fit enough to play but not certain of doing so has presented a tricky dilemma, as much as Iraola would no doubt have preferred for our number 8 to swerve national team duty and prioritise his club instead.

With Hungary not playing until Saturday, that does give Szoboszlai a bit of time to recover from the knee issue he incurred at Selhurst Park, and we’d like to think that Marco Rossi wouldn’t risk fielding him against Georgia unless he’s definitely OK to feature.

While a swift return to action for the 26-year-old would obviously be a good thing, we just hope it doesn’t come at the expense of his involvement for Liverpool in the coming weeks, especially with a hectic run of 11 matches in 40 days before the end of December.

Little sorcerer calls time on playing for his country six weeks after World Cup final defeat which was marred by brutality of his team-mates

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Oliver Brown leads coverage of the greatest events in sport all over the world. He has reported on multiple Olympic Games, World Cups, Ashes series and Super Bowls, plus all major golf and tennis tournaments. His awards include Sports Feature Writer of the Year and Sports Interviewer of the Year. He was named Sports Journalist of the Year in 2024 by the London Press Club. You can find him on X at @oliverbrown_tel.

Lionel Messi’s haunted expression told you more than a three-page retirement statement, artfully displayed alongside a golden pen, ever could. Sobbing and desolate under a cloudless New Jersey sky, he understood that his last game for Argentina had also been among his worst.

Where four years earlier he had adorned the greatest World Cup final with two goals, he found no artistry to salvage this abomination of an encore, drifting into anonymity while his team-mates triggered a bare-knuckle brawl. No wonder he stood apart while Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina did their worst, preferring to absorb one more chorus of adoration from the blue-and-white disciples before forsaking the stage for good.

You could make the case that Messi, as captain of an unholy rabble that had sought only to kick lumps out of Spain, should have taken a moral lead by hauling his team-mates into line, rather than reducing himself to their level by agitating to have Marc Cucurella sent off.

And yet for 20 years, the little sorcerer stayed aloof from his nation’s most lurid antics on the pitch, establishing himself as a strangely beatific presence on whom the highest ideals could be projected. Anybody who has heard Messi’s name being chanted by 50,000 fervent Argentines would have felt it. He was as close as 21st-century sport has come to a secular deity, the object of such veneration that Pope Francis felt compelled to remind Catholics that it was sacrilegious to keep calling him God.

Today, with one agonised announcement, that glorious delirium is over, and already Argentina seems not to know what to do with itself. Pablo Giralt, a sports anchor in Buenos Aires, was unable even to speak when he heard the news live on air, while shattered young fans described how they had called their parents in tears.

Everybody had known the moment was approaching, given the finality of his exit from the final and the subsequent death of his father, Jorge, but it still triggered an unbearable sense of loss.

Messi was the force who galvanised a nation, propelling his side from the unfathomable low of defeat to Saudi Arabia at the 2022 World Cup to holding the trophy aloft 26 days later. Who could ever hope to emulate him, to detonate such joy that the team’s homecoming bus parade in the capital had to be abandoned for a helicopter ride because of the millions on the streets?

“Thank you, God, for making me Argentine,” Messi wrote in his earnest sign-off, his strength of allegiance unfailing to the end. As a veteran of 207 international matches, with his last at La Bombonera distinguished by an ecstatic ovation, he understood both the passions he unleashed among his people and the extent to which his own story became that of an entire country.

You struggled to imagine what life was like in the eye of this madness, with his every move stalked. For the wonder of Messi was that the cult went beyond borders, that the joy he inspired across six World Cups made him beloved to billions. An abiding memory of the 2022 final is of the walk back to the metro station in Doha, where thousands of Nepalese and Bangladeshi supporters, all part of the vast migrant workforce that had built the stadiums, united in “Messi, Messi” refrains even at 1am.

Messi was majestic at that tournament, so imperious in filleting Croatia in the semi-finals that Argentina’s TV reporters abandoned even the pretence of objectivity. “Truly, you made your mark in everyone’s life, and that to me is beyond winning any World Cup,” gushed Sofia Martinez of Television Publica. And when he won it all, the mark only deepened. To occupy any press box at the World Cup where Argentina were involved this summer was to see South American colleagues in “Messi 10” jerseys, helplessly in thrall to his greatness.

As a 39-year-old, he confounded every expectation, scoring a hat-trick against Algeria and breaking Miroslav Klose’s World Cup goals record. Even when engineering those implausible fightbacks against Egypt and England, he held a volatile team together with a minimum of fuss.

Lionel Messi: #FIFAWorldCup edition 🇦🇷🌟 pic.twitter.com/E2xOh3Iose

To study Messi at his last World Cup was to see a man spared the obligation to do anything off the ball. For large periods of each game, the most minutely scrutinised athlete on the planet would do little besides wander around, only to ignite when it mattered most. You saw it in the fateful semi-final with England, where, at 1-0 down, he sloped off to the right touchline as if absent-mindedly gardening. Except he was plotting his opponents’ downfall, working out the precise spots from which to unleash two sumptuous crosses and shatter English hearts.

That alchemy would elude him in the final, where Argentina’s bid for immortality brought only instant notoriety, not to mention £236,000 in fines for misconduct. Was Messi’s image hurt by his connection to the chaos? Not in the long run. Nobody likes to cling to the fact that Pelé’s swansong for Brazil was a drawn friendly with Yugoslavia, or that Diego Maradona bowed out of World Cup football by failing a drug test for ephedrine. What endure are the indelible masterpieces those players bequeathed en route.

It will be the same for Messi, a genius defined less by his ending than by the electrifying adrenalin rush he produced along the way, spanning three finals, 21 goals, and countless flourishes to take the breath away. “Thank you” was all he had left to say. And yet the gratitude, ultimately, is all ours.

#1930. “Cashing in” on Castellanos claim ignores one major stumbling block | West Ham News

Ever since the closing days of the summer transfer window there have been claims that West Ham will be cashing in on Taty Castellanos in the winter: The Argentine has been a huge disappointment in the 15 games of West Ham’s championship season, with just a solitary goal to show for his efforts.

At times he’s resembled more of a moody, disinterested bystander and seems pretty much the most likely player in the eleven to be yellow carded each time he plays.

A solitary goal is plain unacceptable for the frontman who cost £27 million: Claims that he’ll be sold in the winter abound.

Sadly, Everton’s late interest in the summer window, reportedly around £40 million, appears to have evaporated as Taty’s form has waned. Understandably.

Far from happy: One goal in fifteen means Castellanos has been a huge let down in the second tier. Its also means those big money suitors have now evaporated

The newest suggestions from EFL specialist site the72.co.uk suggest Castellanos could be heading back home – however there’s a catch:

“River Plate reportedly view the 28-year-old as a priority target in their striker search, although the finances involved in the deal could prove to be a major hurdle. However, cashing in could give WHUFC the chance to sign a true talisman to aid their promotion bid. “

“Cashing in”? I think not: That’s the elephant in the room here. River Plate have already disclosed that they’ll look at some kind of loan or shared purchase option – as they’re short of funds – which of course will cut no ice with West Ham who will want to replace Taty with a striker more suited to scoring the Championship goals they require.

Merely shipping Taty out on loan without a permanent sale will serve no useful purpose and could actually weaken Scott Parker’s squad. The Hammers have enough loaned – out unwanted stars as it is: Another one added to the list won’t help a rebuild. The only possible route could involve a swap for goal keeper Santiago Beltran – which would still leave the Hammers short of a goal scorer and needing to offload Hermansen or Areola in the winter.

And how often to these player swaps ever come off? Exactly.

#1928. Premier League KMI panel issues emphatic verdict on Alexander Isak penalty decision v Arsenal

The Premier League’s Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel has concluded that Liverpool should’ve had a penalty awarded for an offence by Jurrien Timber on Alexander Isak in their defeat to Arsenal earlier this month.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz scored the only goal of the game at Anfield, the Swedish striker had his shirt pulled in the box by the Gunners defender, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR felt compelled to award a spot kick despite the transgression being clear.

The Reds’ head coach Andoni Iraola went as far as claiming that a penalty would’ve been awarded had our number 9 gone to ground instead of staying on his feet when his jersey was grabbed.

On Wednesday, the Premier League published the findings of several incidents reviewed by the KMI Panel, including the one involving Isak and Timber on 1 November.

Their verdict reads (via premierleague.com): ‘The panel felt that a penalty should have been awarded for a holding action by Timber on Isak, 4:1. One panellist considered the short-lived holding to lack clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress.

‘The majority also felt that VAR should have intervened to recommend an on-field review, 3:2, on the basis that it was a clear and obvious error. Two panellists considered that the subjectivity in assessing impact meant this did not meet the high threshold for VAR intervention.’

The KMI Panel concluded: ‘In this instance the panel deemed that Timber’s challenge on Isak met the threshold for a holding offence and should have resulted in a penalty kick, both on-field and through VAR intervention.’

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

How nice of the KMI Panel to come back and tell us what was so damn obvious at the time of the incident – or at least obvious to anyone not named Andy Madley or Stuart Attwell, or whichever member of the panel felt that the right decision was made on the day.

How that individual concluded that Timber’s actions lacked ‘clear impact on the ability of Isak to progress’ is baffling – the Liverpool striker would surely have gotten on the end of Bradley Barcola’s cross had his shirt not been so blatantly pulled.

The panel’s verdict today won’t come as much consolation to anyone involved with the Reds, who were deprived of a legitimate penalty which – if converted – could’ve significantly altered the course of a match that they lost 1-0.

It’s not much good being told in retrospect that the officials got it wrong; these are clear decisions that professional referees should be capable of getting correct at the time, especially when they have the fallback option of VAR.

We get that many incidents are subjective and that consensus will never be achieved when it comes to refereeing in the Premier League, but there’s simply no excuse for botching calls like the Timber/Isak incident 10 days ago.

Published: 13:14 EST, 9 November 2026 | Updated: 13:15 EST, 9 November 2026

Wayne Rooney has led the praise for football super-agent Paul Stretford as the industry heavyweight was honoured at the Global Football Industry Awards.

Stretford, alongside Kenneth Shepherd, received the prestigious Lifetime Achievement Award at this year's Awards in recognition of their longstanding careers and work on Soccer Aid for Unicef.

He has worked by Rooney's side for more than 20 years, and has recently appeared on the former footballer's reality TV show, which he fronts alongside wife Coleen.

Rooney presented Stretford with the award himself, alongside Toni Duggan and comedian Paddy McGuinness. Theo Walcott and Jamie Carragher hosted the ceremony.

Rooney said of his agent and close friend: 'Paul in particular has had a major influence on my life since I was a teenager and has guided my career.

'Both Paul and Kenneth are very deserving of this award. It is not before time and I'm delighted for both of them. The work they've done on Soccer Aid is phenomenal too.'

Wayne Rooney (centre) has lauded close friend and football super agent Paul Stretford (right)

Stretford doesn't just look after Rooney, having also worked with the likes of Harry Maguire since founding Proactive Sports Management, now known as Triple S Sports Group, in 1987.

Shepherd, meanwhile, has been instrumental in the success of the Soccer Aid initiative which has raised more than £137million for Unicef since it launched in 2006.

McGuinness added: 'I'm so proud to pay tribute to a duo who have had a profound impact on football and two figures we've both had the pleasure of working with over the years. Together, they built the Triple S Group into a dynamic force in British and international football.'

England assistant manager Anthony Barry also carried out an exclusive Q&A at the event, which saw Tyler Alexander-Arnold, brother of England defender Trent, also scoop a top award.

The brother of the Real Madrid star represents Jordan Henderson, Jarrod Bowen and Andy Robertson as well as his sibling, who saw his PLG Agency bought by Gersh talent agency in May of this year.

According to the NY Times’ fan survey, the biggest consensus was not for the approval of the new manager – although there is a pretty strong 77% majority of fans who responded who give the appointment of Scott Parker the thumbs up.

Likeable yes, dependable no: 85% of West Ham fans want Hermansen out of the team

Eighty five percent of fans have had enough of the Dane’s inept performances in between the sticks, with one fan driven to comment that West Ham’s goal would be better defended simply by hanging a green jersey on the cross bar rather than continuing to select the out of form Hermansen.

Of course the fly in the ointment is that Areola has been reported as ‘unfit’ – whether that means third choice Finlay Herrick comes into consideration – who can say- but it’d be a brave selection for Parker to leave his number one on the bench if Areola isn’t ready for the Preston North End fixture next weekend, however much it seems supporters want to see Hermansen out of the team.

The Brighton goalkeeper was reportedly among a shortlist of candidates being considered by the Reds prior to the summer transfer window, with the Merseysiders eventually agreeing a deal to sign Lucca Brughmans, who’ll join from Genk next summer.

Verbruggen – who’s currently with the Netherlands squad for their concluding UEFA Nations League fixtures – has insisted that despite the rumoured interest from Liverpool, he’s more than happy with the Seagulls, who currently sit second in the Premier League.

The 24-year-old said (via NOS): “Right now we’re doing really well at Brighton, so it would be a real shame to ruin that by living in the future. I really try to stay in the moment, to focus on what is currently going on. I enjoy that, and that is also how I perform best.”

Brighton’s magnificent season so far has been underpinned by the excellence of the man between the sticks, who’s kept seven clean sheets in 10 league games and conceded just three times in eight top-flight matches since a 4-3 defeat at Chelsea in August (Transfermarkt).

Figures from Fotmob show that he’s prevented 4.39 xG worth of goals for his team, more than anyone else in the Premier League, and he put in a heroic display in the Seagulls’ recent win at Manchester City as he recorded no fewer than seven saves (Sky Sports).

Giorgi Mamardashvili was signed with the intention of succeeding the Brazilian eventually, although the 26-year-old hasn’t always convinced during his time with the Reds so far, and Brughmans will add to the queue once he joins ahead of next season.

Right now there wouldn’t seem to be any urgent need for LFC to move heaven and earth to sign Verbruggen, but if circumstances were to change regarding their current goalkeeping options, it could be worth keeping a hand in should the opportunity arise to move for the Brighton stopper.

#1922. Joe Hart pinpoints ‘unbelievable’ Alisson Becker trait which makes him ‘one of the best’

Joe Hart has proclaimed that Alisson Becker will ‘forever be regarded as one of the best’ goalkeepers to have graced the Premier League.

Liverpool’s number 1 has been rightly acknowledged as one of the foremost players in his position in world football since his move to Anfield in 2018 and has been pivotal towards the trophies won by the Reds in that time.

He produced one of his greatest LFC performances in the victory at Crystal Palace last weekend, with his tally of six saves including a world-class reaction stop from Daichi Kamada which left the Eagles attacker astounded.

In an interview with The Athletic, Hart lavished praise on Alisson for the consistency he’s shown throughout his time in England, and especially his prowess in one-on-saves.

The ex-Manchester City stopper said of the 34-year-old: “One of the best to do it in the Premier League. What I love is his simplicity. He’s not necessarily eye-catching in the way he moves, but it’s the way he deals with everything.

“He makes massive saves. His one-on-one technique is unbelievable, and he has made it his own. He very rarely gets beaten one-on-one, which in this Premier League is incredible because you’re up against some of the best strikers in the world.

“He’s struggled a bit with injuries lately, but I think he’ll forever be regarded as one of the best to play the position.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Last weekend, Alisson produced a perfect example of the one-on-one ability that Hart pinpointed by thwarting Yeremy Pino when the Crystal Palace forward was through on goal, a significant intervention at a time that Liverpool were 2-0 up.

When it comes to ‘massive saves’, it mightn’t quite be in the same category as his legendary stoppage-time heroics against Napoli in December 2018 when our Champions League campaign was in the balance, but it showed that the 34-year-old remains a world-class goalkeeper.

His outstanding display at Selhurst Park came after a couple of costly misjudgements in defeats to Arsenal and Fenerbahce, which shows the Brazilian’s strength of character to put those unfortunate moments behind him and come up trumps for his team.

Alisson’s agent Ze Maria revealed in recent days that talks have begun over a prospective contract renewal at Liverpool, with the Reds’ number 1 having said after the win at Palace that he’d like to stay at Anfield beyond the expiry of his current deal next summer.

More heroics like those he produced in south London four days ago, and an extension to his existing terms should be a no-brainer for sporting director Julian Ward.
