#1839. Scotland are failing to dispel emperor’s new clothes concerns after laboured victory

The Scottish Football Association’s ticket promotion drive for this match emphasised that games are always better under the lights. They might need to re-think that one.

This was another endurance test that at least had a satisfactory outcome, courtesy of John McGinn’s double. In between times a goal for North Macedonia - their first in nine games - probably triggered a national holiday back home and made things look very difficult indeed for Sebastien Pocognoli.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Scotland held onto their lead, given to them after McGinn drove into the box following strong centre-forward play from Che Adams, for the best part of three minutes.

A penalty, awarded after a VAR check a good couple of minutes after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski's trip on Ben Gannon-Doak occurred, saved Scotland’s blushes with 16 minutes left and kept their Nations League hopes just about alive.

McGinn did the necessary from the spot although Oli McBurnie, who had replaced Adams six minutes earlier, might have appreciated being given the ball in his seemingly eternal quest for an international goal. It was perhaps too important a kick to take any chances. A manager’s future prospects might have rested on it.

It was a case of third time lucky for Pocognoli as he secured his first Hampden win on what had not seemed like a particularly auspicious date. For the first time since the notorious 0-0 draw against Uruguay that torpedoed their 1986 World Cup, Scotland were in action on a Friday the 13th. What could possibly go wrong? A lot, it seemed at times.

If anything underlined that these are very different times for Scotland it was the sight of Scott McTominay, almost a year to the day since that overhead kick against Denmark, launching himself into the air again in an effort to meet Gilmour’s cross. Although he connected well, the direction was lacking. The ball went high over the bar.

There was no goal from the halfway line this time either. Instead, we were treated to one of the worst misses ever seen at Hampden when Gilmour skied the ball from seven yards seconds after the interval.

The Hampden crowd was getting testy. Boos had greeted the half-time whistle, with the score still goalless and the hosts perhaps lucky not to have conceded.

McGinn’s opener ten minutes after half-time seemed like just the medicine. However, underlining how this was never straightforward, Macedonia equalised almost immediately. They had to score a goal sometime but it was not a good look for Scotland or McTominay, who was beaten in the air at the front post by Elmin Rastodar following a corner.

A clumsy challenge at the other end by Dimitrievski on Gannon-Doak, whose poor touch had already looked to have taken the chance away from him, gave Scotland the gratifying chance to equalise from the spot 17 minutes later.

The hosts had endured an uncertain start that was a decent indicator of what lay ahead. What seemed like teething problems might have been attributed to a defence playing together for the first time. Ryan Porteous was brought back into the starting line-up, his first start since the opening match of Euro 2024 when he was sent off.

Luke Graham, meanwhile, earned his second cap - a first start for Scotland - and was planted right in the middle of the three-man backline. After surviving a few shaky moments initially, the Stoke City defender acquitted himself superbly well.

North Macedonia’s dismal run, which included not having scored in this Nations League campaign so far, perhaps convinced Pocognoli he could make such alterations though injury had restricted his options. Poertoeus, though, hadn’t even been named in the original squad.

Defence wasn’t expected to be an issue. It was a Friday night after a long week at work. Fans wanted to be entertained, they wanted to see some tangible evidence of a new Scotland they have been promised. Pocognoli might wear a suit very well but he’s not proved himself to be his predecessor’s equal at obtaining results, although this was more like it. The fear is that this supposedly more free-flowing Scotland has made them blunter. The phrase the emperor’s new clothes could not be banished from the mind.

Not even McTominay could ignite things. He seemed ready to burst the net just a few minutes later after Lewis Ferguson’s header found the Napoli midfielder with his back to goal in the box. When he turned, it looked like there would be only one outcome. However, Dimitrievski made a tremendous save low to his left.

Yes, this was another occasion where the North Macedonian goalkeeper excelled himself, just as he did in Skopje at the start of last month.

Another save, when he plucked a deflected Adams header out from beneath his crossbar, was even better. There were mitigating factors for Scotland failing to make the breakthrough in the opening half.

It might have been worse for the home team. A cute lay-off from Darko Churlinov set up skipper Enis Bardhi, who lashed a left-footed shot into the side-netting. Most of the Hampden crowd feared the ball had gone in. The smattering of North Macedonia fans were beside themselves.

Sadly for them, happily for the vast majority, the rippling effect was due to the ball hitting the wrong side of the net. It might have been marginally offside in any case. Jeers greeted the blowing of the half-time whistle moments later, nonetheless.

Would Scotland come out with a renewed sense of purpose? It seemed so. Adams pounced on a short pass back and cut the ball back while Dimitrievski dithered.

Billy Gilmour is no one’s idea of a prolific goalscorer but even he couldn’t miss from seven yards, goal gaping. He did. Quite incredibly, the ball comfortably cleared the bar. People were referencing Chris Iwelumo, meaning it was one of the worst misses of all time. It was at the right end, certainly. McGinn showed him how to do it, moving level with Hughie Gallacher in third place on 24 goals in the all-time list of goalscorers and ensuring Andy Robertson’s record-equalling 102nd cap would also be the victorious one the skipper deserved.

#1838. ‘I won £125,000 on the Postcode Lottery - all I want is a Leeds United season ticket again’

Pauline Place had to give up her season ticket 12 years ago and now dreams of getting a new one with her daughter after claiming the windfall when postcode WF6 2ST was named as this week’s Millionaire Street draw.

She shared the £1m jackpot with seven of her Altofts neighbours, while nearby Wakefield Hospital has also got a £75,000 cash injection thanks to Postcode Lottery.

Upon learning of her win, Pauline only had one objective on her mind.

She said: “I started supporting Leeds United in 1964. I changed jobs and started going to games with the people I worked with.

Among the other winners on the cul-de-sac in Altofts was Jade Williams, 40, and her wife Ruth, 38.

Delighted ticket holder Jade, a clinical nurse specialist in a stroke unit, said: “It feels like we give so much to our jobs; it’s a 24/7, really demanding job. This feels like it is a reward back to us for looking after acutely ill people.”

Ruth, an orthopaedics ward manager, added: “The job is rewarding and fulfilling, and this is too – but in a completely different way.”

Yorkshire appears to be on something of a lucky run with the Postcode Lottery at the moment, with this being the fifth time in as many weeks the region has won big.

Last month, 20 neighbours in the tiny village of Birdsedge – 17 miles away – shared the same £1m prize, while two neighbours in Bridlington shared £750,000 in the monthly draw.

Also in October, one player bagged £378,272 after HG3 4AP won the Millionaire Street prize in Dacre, near Harrogate. Eighty eight others split the remainder of the £1m pot in the wider HG3 4 sector.

#1836. Maitland-Niles’ last-gasp debut goal salvages Everton’s miserable week

At the final whistle, the first song the stadium DJ played was Spirit of the Blues and how those relieved Evertonians lapped it up after a week of angst.

Their team had been on the precipice of a defeat that would have exacerbated all the frustrations that bubbled away following the chaotic conclusion to the transfer window. Indeed, it was 10 seconds over the allotted five minutes of added time when the ball fell to Ainsley Maitland-Niles.

It had been three years since the former Arsenal full-back had played in the Premier League – his last goal in England was on October 30, 2019, in an EFL Cup tie with Liverpool at Anfield that ended 5-5 – and he would not have joined Everton if their attempt to sign Kenny Tete from Fulham had not failed.

But here he was 30 yards from goal, with no need to break his stride as Manchester United’s backtracking defenders presented him with an invitation to shoot. So that’s what he did. With one perfectly timed swish of his right foot, an unlikely hero transformed the mood of a club.

"That is something SPECIAL!"Ainsley Maitland-Niles earns a draw for Everton on his debut with an unbelievable 96th minute strike! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/HNdx9PxrUP

“Brilliant technique,” said David Moyes, Everton’s manager, who had only introduced Maitland-Niles in the 77th minute after James Garner had succumbed to cramp and could run no more. “We are still getting to know Ainsley but that was a brilliant goal.”

Only those with the coldest hearts would begrudge Everton this point, which was especially hard-earned given they had conceded an 88th-minute header to Benjamin Sesko. But there is no chance a disbelieving Michael Carrick will feel that way.

Benajmin Sesko puts Manchester United back in front! 👊 pic.twitter.com/MF3A9LyaY8

United should, really, have won this game comfortably. Everton were there to be exploited and when Bryan Mbuemo put them ahead early in the second half, they should have powered away into the distance. Everton’s effort was good but they were in danger of losing hope.

Yet, incredibly, United gave Everton two helping hands. They had not been in a position to assist last Tuesday evening, when phone calls from Merseyside to Old Trafford to take Joshua Zirkzee on loan were met with rejection. But the second half display more than made up for that.

“We’re bitterly disappointed,” said Carrick, who was one step removed from having steam puffing from his ears. “All the work that went into putting us in that position at different stages to then come away like that… it’s not a great feeling. It feels like a defeat. It’s a bit of a cliché to say.”

But clichés are true. First United were passive when Tyrique George crashed in a brilliant right-footed drive in the 83rd minute and then, after Sesko profited from Jordan Pickford’s weak hands, they were passive again in allowing Everton to build the move that ended up with Maitland-Niles’ howitzer.

How had it come to this? It was beautiful bedlam, the kind of joy that only football delivers, but for long periods it felt like it was an opportunity for United. There was anticipation that Everton’s fans would create a furnace but there was also the fear it would be dispiritingly quiet.

Had this fixture been at Goodison Park, with its steep stands, tight confines and acoustics that split your ears, United would have been aware of the siege mentality as soon as their bus rolled up outside the stadium but their new sparkling home is rather more hospitable.

This is no criticism of the home crowd – it is anything but. Why should it always fall to them to bail out the failings of those in charge when those in charge, specifically the executives and recruitment department, have given them scant reason to have hope?

The route to victory for United, then, was relatively straightforward: for all Everton’s initial huff and puff, it always appeared that it would be a case of the away team repeating the simple things, retaining their concentration and waiting for a breakthrough.

It could have come as early as the eighth minute. Luke Shaw’s deep cross to the back post picked out Mbuemo, whose cushioned header invited Bruno Fernandes to take aim but the Portuguese’s volley clipped the crossbar with Pickford stranded.

United dominated and Marcus Rashford was central to it all, a scampering presence down the left who gave Merlin Röhl, playing as an auxiliary right-back, all kinds of problems. The only thing missing from his opening 45 minutes was a goal.

When Mbuemo scored so early after the break, it felt as if this was going to be one puncture too many for Everton to withstand and the anticipation was United would get the job done. In all fairness to Moyes, however, he was not in the mood to accept excuses.

His substitutions were all positive, with Jack Grealish changing the mood and Hayden Hackney providing dynamism. But it was the former Middlesbrough man who drove forward to give George, whose loan move from Chelsea was made permanent in June, the opportunity to smash an 83rd-minute bullet past Senne Lammens.

"That was unanswerable!"What a way for Tyrique George to open his account for Everton! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/c0HPRjWUia

“I told the players there would be no excuses and the players all agreed,” Moyes said. “They have hugely bought into it. And, you know, sometimes when you have [fewer] players it means everybody has to be ready. Sometimes when you have a small squad you have to find a way of making it work.”

They did just that. Pickford should have saved the header from Sesko that looked as though it had given United the lift, but Everton, with their manager belligerent and their fans sensing all was not lost, had other ideas. The noise they generated as Maitland-Niles’s goal went in was unique to this stadium.

As Moyes celebrated, shaking his fists and revelling in the positive turn of events, Carrick put his hand across his face and shook his head repeatedly. All the while, Everton’s fans sang I guess that’s why they call it the Blues. United’s head coach certainly had them. Everton, simply, had relief.

2 - For just the second time in the last 50 years, Manchester United have conceded 2+ goals in each of their first three games of a league season, along with 2020-21.Leaky. pic.twitter.com/B2Dk6Ioxkq

It felt like a win. The crowd was with us, we fight to the end and that’s how you get that type of result.

It’s amazing. Everyone wants to start like that and fortunately I did. I put my foot through it and it ended up in the top corner which I’m happy about.

I came here to work hard. It’s a team full of hard workers and I fit right in. I’m going to show I can pull my weight and give as much as everyone else, if not a little bit more.

Even I have a lump in my throat to see him do that after his original move to Everton in August 2021 was stymied by a late change of heart by Mikel Arteta. Don’t normally approve of badge kissers but he has waited such a long time for that and must have thought his chance had gone.

Just time to kick off before the whistle goes. Probably a fair result and that goal from Maitland-Niles was good enough to win a game never mind save it.

Everton 2 Manchester United 2 (Maitland-Niles) Stunning strike! Mazraoui had tackled Dewsbury-Hall in the box after more good work between Grealish and Hackney down the left. But the tackle diverted the ball to Maitland-Niles 25 yards out. And he wrapped his instep around a shot on debut that bent into the top left corner. What a goal!

"That is something SPECIAL!"Ainsley Maitland-Niles earns a draw for Everton on his debut with an unbelievable 96th minute strike! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/HNdx9PxrUP

Grealish’s beguiling feet dazzle Mazraoui down the Everton left as he tricks him to reach the byline. He cuts back a pass to Barry who tees up Hackney for a shot that he wafts miles over the bar. Grealish gives him a look as if to say, “Really?”

George finds himself in a near identical spot from which he scored and tries again with a thumping shot that flies into the side-netting via Lammens’ finger tips. He was offside on this occasion, though.

Five minutes of added time for Everton to level again.

Everton 1 Manchester United 2 (Sesko) Sesko wins the ball in the middle and works it out to Bruno Fernandes running down the left. He stops, faces up Maitland-Niles and waits for Shaw to gallop past him before rolling it into the left-back’s stride. Shaw fizzes over a cross that parts Tarkowski’s luxuriant barnet and Sesko, lurking on his shoulder, buries it from eight yards.

Benajmin Sesko puts Manchester United back in front! 👊 pic.twitter.com/MF3A9LyaY8

As Dominic says, below, Manchester United have been asking for this. They have been toothless since Mbeumo’s goal and the only significant threat, Rashford, was taken off for a left-back.

Everton 1 Man Utd 1 (George) A rasping, rising shot that beats Lammens at his near post. He absolutely larruped it after good work by Hackney to put him in space down the right of the box.

"That was unanswerable!"What a way for Tyrique George to open his account for Everton! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/c0HPRjWUia

If you largely try and defend a 1-0 lead and don’t go for that second goal, there’s always the danger of that happening. Superb finish from George to equalise but it’s been so passive from United. Asking for trouble and they’ve got it. Big 7 minutes plus injury time for them now.

Free-kick on the left, parallel with the penalty spot. Hackney bends it in with his right and Branthwaite heads it on target but too close to Lammens who oddly elects to punch.

Mykolenko gives the ball back from the throw-in as Fernandes serves his minute on the sidelines.

Dalot is booked for pulling Grealish’s shirt when the left winger had spun him.

Maitland-Niles receives a warm reception. I had forgotten that he has five England caps.

Bruno Fernandes goes down after kicking Tarkowski’s studs when his foot was raised. The referee does not stop play but books Maguire for complaining when the ball eventually goes out.

Garner almost immediately goes down and starts stretching his calves.

Mykolenko hurls a long throw into the Man Utd box. Dewsbury-Hall meets it with a shot that he catches sweetly but hits a defender. The ball rebounds to Armstrong who scuffs his attempt wide .

George has switched to the right to accommodate Grealish. I wonder if there was ever a possibility of him returning to Villa? Would Unai Emery treasure him?

“He’s back!” the stadium announcer has proclaimed, as Jack Grealish has entered the fray. The move has provided an immediate bounce but let’s see what the former England man can do to change the pattern of the game. Everton believe they have got a £100m player. It’s time to show it.

Grealish’s first contribution sends Mykolenko away on an overlap and Martinez messes up his clearance from the cross, shanking it behind for a corner that they defend soundly.

Manchester United corner on the left after Tielemans’ 25-yard shot was deflected behind. Fernandes plays it along the ground to Shaw in the D. The left-back’s control spoons the ball up with his left so he improvises a right-foot volley with his swinger, dragging it predictably wide.

Rohl is beaten yet again by Rashford and works his way into the book after pulling him back. It’s been hard going for the Everton right back against Rashford but United just haven’t taken advantage of it enough.

Jack Grealish is stripped and ready to come on.

Rashford jinks at pace 35 yards up the inside-left channel, chopping to the left and barrelling between defenders. He takes it too wide to shoot so cutely backheels to Cunha who pulls back his left foot to shoot from six yards but Tarkowski slides his leg through his gait and pokes the ball away. The away fans shout for a penalty but Cunha has no complaints.

Barry diddles Martinez by feinting to the right and then darting left to open a rout to goal. He hammers a shot from about 16 yards that Shaw slides across to block, diverting it to Dewsbury-Hall whose follow-up effort is a tame daisycutter that Lammens easily gathers.

It threatened to be the case that a Manchester United goal would puncture the atmosphere completely and so it has proven. The likelihood here is the away team will score again in the next 10 minutes to completely kill the game. Everton have endured a miserable week and this flat performance is entirely in keeping with the narrative.

Johnson cuts in off the right to run on to Garner’s pass and shoots from 18 yards. Martinez makes himself as big as possible and the shot clips his calf, sending it up before it dips threateningly, whistling over the bar.

Mbeumo heads out Garner’s corner. Dewsbury-Hall crosses it back into the box and Tarkowski tries to head it across into the middle. Manchester United clear their lines.

Shaw slides in to block Dewsbury-Hall’s shot after the attacking midfielder had manipulated an opportunity with a quick interchange with Johnson.

Key for Manchester United, who have taken the lead in a match for the first time this season, not to let up on the tempo with which they started this half.

Everton respond with a menacing cross in from the left, from George, I think, that eludes Johnson as he arrives in the middle a second late.

Everton 0 Manchester United 1 (Mbeumo) United were probing patiently from the kick-off, Mainoo the hub until he helped the ball down the right and Mbeumo drove in from the right touchline, splitting George and Mykolenko until he reached the 18-yard line and wrapped his left instep around a shot that he arrowed into the bottom left corner.

A brilliant run and a fine finish from Bryan Mbeumo! 👏 pic.twitter.com/IM9kVcdPkh

We hadn’t seen that Mbeumo in the first half – so much better, driving inside at pace and with intent. Good decoy run from Fernandes. Top finish from Mbeumo.

Both managers will want to see a lot more urgency from their sides in the second half. Rashford has been United’s most threatening outlet and has the beating of Rohl but Mbeumo and Cunha were poor in those opening 45 minutes and both guilty of turning over the ball cheaply when United were breaking late in the first period. Barry should have hit the target with a header from Rohl’s cross. But it’s been a lacklustre game, low in quality so far.

A drab match that came to life in the last few minutes of the half, creating good a good chance for Thierno Barry and Jarrad Branthwaite thwarting Marcus Rashford and Bruno Fernandes. Everton look wide open on the right side of their defence and Brennan Johnson is starting to make headway against Luke Shaw.

Brilliant sliding tackle from Branthwaite when Rashford, piling down the inside-left channel in full flight. Just as he was about to pull the trigger, Branthwaite launched himself to knock it away and leapt back to his feet to block Fernandes’ stinging follow-up with the his head.

Mykolenko’s long throw from the left raises the Man Utd blood pressure as they try to scramble it clear. The ball pinballs around the six-yard box, comes off Dalot last and straight to Branthwaite who catches it straight and true but clips the shot at Lammens.

There will be three additional minutes. Barry and Johnson link up again to send the rangey striker down the right but again he hits his cross/shot straight at a defender at close quarters. He can’t work an angle but tries to go through a defender.

Rohl and Barry link up in more orthodox fashion with an excellent, dipping cross from the right-back. Barry peels off Maguire and thumps his header wide. That’s the best chance of the game.

Neat one-two between Johnson and Barry sends the latter into the box on the right but his shot/cross is fired straight at Shaw. The crowd shouts ‘Hand ball!’ but it wasn’t and the ref waves play on.

Everton have had no spark at all so far. George goes down when challenged by Mbeumo to give them a free-kick on the left, 35 yards from goal. Garner hits a floaty cross to the right of the box and Barry heads it wide.

It was Johnson who was under scrutiny for a ‘foul’ on Martinez’ but it was just a hand on the back.

Branthwaite is winded when he collides with Pickford in midair defending a back-post cross. Seems to be OK.

Fernandes whips over a cross and Armstrong beats Martínez to head it clear. VAR is looking at Martínez’s claim that he was fouled. Now it’s been cleared.

Yellow card for Johnson for sliding into Cunha’s stride and raising his right boot to leg him up right by the byline on the left, 12 inches outside the area.

Shaw trips Rohl in the Everton penalty area as they fought for the ball from Branthwaite’s block of Rashford’s superb cross from the left. The winger was looking for a near-post runner but Branthwaite read it perfectly, certainly better than Cunha, and telescoped out a leg to intercept.

Given the chaotic end to Everton’s transfer window, the atmosphere was going to go one of two ways: bearpit or flat as a pancake. As of now, it’s very much the latter situation, and not even a first sight of Jack Grealish has enabled the volume to be pumped up. Everton are finding it difficult and special attention will need to be paid to Harrison Armstrong, who has been harshly booked but must now walk a disciplinary tightrope. The young midfielder has played encouragingly once again and is desperate to impress.

Ripples of applause for Grealish who comes off the bench to warm up. Armstrong is urged to shoot when fed by Garner’s curling pass up the inside-right channel. But he dithers and then plays it out to Johnson whose cross is no good.

Best move of the game to date should have ended with Cunha hitting the target. The silkiest bit about it was how Rashford lulled Rohl into a false sense of security with his first touch then tapped the ball past him in the next movement just as Rohl was engaging. Very clever.

Now Shaw reaches the byline down the left and cuts it back for Fernandes. Branthwaite again to the rescue, diligently doing his job and closing down the Man Utd captain. Merlin Röhl is a talented player but he’s no right-back against the well-grooved Rashford and Shaw combo.

Dalot let the Rashford pass through his legs to Cunha, probably deliberately but he might have been better placed to apply the finish himself. Cunha had the time and space to do much better than he did, though.

Cunha blazes a side-foot shot from 18 yards over the bar. It was put on a plate by Rashford’s cut-back from the byline after the winger was sent down the flank by Mbeumo’s clever pass.

Manchester united again open up Everton through the middle when Mainoo slips a pass to Bruno Fernandes who puts his laces through a 25-yard shot that Branthwaite bravely throws himself at and deflects wide and out for a corner.

Tielemans’ eyes widen as space opens up between Armstrong and Garner but he scuffs his 22-yard shot which floats gently down Pickford’s throat.

Shaw cuts out Branthwaite’s long pass to Armstrong who was running down the inside-left channel. Manchester United do not clear their lines convincingly and Everton come back at them, probing away with George and Armstrong.

Dalot is let off a booking inexplicably for pulling George’s arm after being spun by Everton’s left-winger. The crowd is irate at that and seething even more when Armstrong is yellow-carded moments later for wrapping an arm around Fernandes’ neck to stop him running away.

Big shout for a home penalty when Barry goes down, face first in the six-yard box when closed down ny Martínez but it was more of a belly flop than a foul.

Slick attacking move from Manchester United, zipping a dozen passes around Everton and ending with Shaw being slid down the left by Rashford. The left-back crosses from the byline and Mbeumo cushions a header to Bruno Fernandes who flashes a sidewinder volley into the crossbar.

In the grand scheme of things, this might sound the most ridiculous complaint you have read but Manchester United’s kit - really? When they play away at Everton, their kit has always been – and always should be – red shirts, black shorts and black socks. It looks odd with two teams playing in white shorts. This may seem a random observation but there we go... there hasn’t been any action to discuss in the opening four minutes!

Maguire returns to the fray as Everton pass the ball through midfield to Johnson on the right. His cross, aiming for Barry, is cut out by Maguire and cleared to halfway. Back come Everton until Dewsbury-Hall is too rough with Mainoo as the Man Utd midfielder tackled him. Free-kick.

Lammens kicks the ball the full length of the field and Pickford picks it up. Mbeumo momentarily is at right-back with Dalot at centre-half.

Maguire is OK to continue but he will be off the field for the mandatory minute.

Maguire headed the back of Barry’s head and splattered his nose. He should be all right though he might need the cotton wool nostril bungs for a while, like Blackadder, the pencils and ‘wibble’.

Big cheers goes around the stadium when Harrison Armstrong’s name has read out. Everton would likely have sold him had there not been a backlash from fans opposing his sale.

Concern here for Harry Maguire. Looks in distress on the ground, laying very still. Concerned players around.

Leny Yoro is warming up on the touchline.

Looks like he caught the back of Barry’s head as he went to challenge. Sat up nose receiving treatment on a very bloodied nose.

Everton kick off, attacking from right to left. The fans, as usual, are making a racket. Everton work the ball back to Pickford who clips a diagonal up the left. Everton play it towards Barry who collides with Maguire who takes a blow to the head.

The teams emerge from the tunnel, both teams in their home kits with the only twist Manchester United’s switch to white socks.

We’re looking forward to seeing what [Brennan Johnson] does. We know he is very capable [and shown it] in recent seasons. Let’s hope he can bring us goals and assists as he did for Tottenham.

We’ve needed them [the two deadline day signings]. Maitland-Niles is physically fine. I don’t think Jack should be yet. We’ve needed it.

That’s all gone now [deadline day]. It’s all about the football. That’s what people are coming to see and we’ll have to play as well as we have done in our opening two games, get a positive result. Hopefully we can continue to build on it.

Nothing different [expected from the fans today]. They’re always really good for us.

No surprise United remain unchanged from the 5-2 win over Ipswich although Carrick will be looking for his side to score first here and make life a little easier for themselves after going behind to Hull and Ipswich in their opening two games. Brennan Johnson comes in for the departed Iliman Ndiaye, who joined Manchester City for £65m on deadline day. Jack Grealish is on the bench for Everton.

Moyes issued a call to arms to Everton fans in his programme notes after a dismal transfer window that has left him with just 18 outfield players. The Everton manager warning there may be difficult times to come.

“Finally, I must stress the importance of us all pulling together,” Moyes wrote.

“We need to be strong again and there may be occasions when we may have to find a way to get through some difficult moments.

“It is something you have all done in recent seasons. Everyone has pulled together for the good of the football club and we may need to do so again.”

We did a lot of good things [against Ipswich]. No two games are ever the same. We have different challenges today. We have to be ready for that with some slightly different ideas. But the boys did well last week, trained well this week and we’re really looking forward to it.

The next result is always the most important one regardless of what’s happened. Building momentum, building a run, of course it’s important. It’s game-by-game, as you know, but this is as tough as it comes for us, Everton away.

It’s not a major deal, we’ve got the squad and we can cope with it [increase in numbers of fixtures with the return to European football].

Everton  Pickford; Röhl, Tarkowski, Branthwaite, Mykolenko; Armstrong, Garner; Johnson, Dewsbury-Hall, George; Barry. Substitutes Travers, Maitland-Niles, Keane, Grealish, O’Brien, Dibling, Alcaraz, Hackney, Graham.

Man Utd  Lammens; Dalot, Maguire, Martínez, Shaw; Tielemans, Mainoo; Mbeumo, Fernandes, Rashford; Cunha. Substitutes Darlow, Mazraoui, Mount, Zirkzee, Dorgu, Yoro, Santos, Heaven, Sesko.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of Everton vs Manchester United from Hill Dickinson Stadium. The hosts have made a creditable start on the field but four points from their opening two games cannot gloss over the discontent fostered by the owners and executives because of the credibility gap between their talk about recruitment and their paltry achievements.

The fact that their comeback against Bournemouth to earn a draw last week was achieved with Beto, Tim Iroegbunum and Iliman Ndiaye on the field and all three have now been sold with only Jack Grealish returning on loan to compensate tells its own story.

Speak to supporters and it is emblematic of ownership, they fear, who are prioritising Roma and view the Hill Dickinson as a terrific multisport and concert venue with a heritage football club attached. The bullishness of Angus Kinnear, the chief executive, rings hollower with each pronouncement and it is little wonder that the fans are so disenchanted.

David Moyes will not walk away but once again he has been sent into the fray against teams with £250m midfields armed with a spud gun. Having said that, we should not underestimate his capacity to rally the old “dogs of war” spirit even if the crowd is still yearning more for a “school of science” revival.

Manchester United won on their first visit to the Hill Dickinson last season when Benjamin Sesko came off the bench to score the only goal of the game and give Michael Carrick a fifth win in six league games as caretaker manager. They were far more fluid in their forward play during the victory over Ipswich last week but it was against an error-stricken defence and they continued to be as worryingly open at the back as they had been against Hull City in the opening round of fixtures with Luke Shaw and Lisandro Martínez having brain fades.

Shaw is a doubt today, along with Mason Mount, while Amad Diallo, Matthijs de Ligt, Carlos Baleba and Manuel Ugarte have all been ruled out. Only Christian Norgaard is absent for Everton but so thin is their squad, they will cast covetous glances at Man Utd’s bench, not least at Joshua Zirkzee who was the subject of a very late rejected bid on deadline day.

#1835. Sebastien Pocognoli predicts another Scotland record will be broken and identifies ‘something we need to fix’

Sebastien Pocognoli believes it is only a matter of time until John McGinn becomes Scotland’s all-time top goalscorer.

The Scotland manager saw McGinn score a match-winning double to help Scotland secure a scratchy and often uninspired win over North Macedonia. It handed Pocognoli his first Hampden victory at the third attempt and brought some relief for the Belgian.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

It hadn’t looked good when North Macedonia equalised almost immediately after McGinn had put Scotland ahead after 54 minutes. The header from Elmin Rastoder was the visitors' first goal in nine games.

A penalty from McGinn following a VAR check with 16 minutes left, after goalkeeper Stole Dimitrievski clumsily tripped Ben Gannon-Doak, secured the three points for Scotland and kept their hopes of finishing second in their Nations League group alive. Slovenia drew 0-0 with group winners Switzerland.

Pocognoli’s side must win against Switzerland in St Gallen on Monday and hope Macedonia take something from their clash at home against the Slovenians.

With McGinn in the side, anything is possible against Switzerland. Pocognoli hailed the Aston Villa’s contribution and feels he will shortly overtake Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law in the rankings. Both legends scored 30 goals for Scotland and McGinn, who now sits third with Hughie Gallacher on 24 goals, is now just seven goals from overtaking the pair at the top. He has already scored three goals under Pocognoli, having struck a penalty in the 2-0 win against North Macedonia in Skopje last month.

“I'm more focused on the collective challenge and goals,” said Pocognoli. “And I believe if we can build something nice around the collective, then John will one day break the record. He has had a lot of chances through these five games together already. It's important but the individual record I always bring in the collective package. And I hope for him that he can reach it.”

Pocognoli, if not satisfied with all aspects of Scotland’s play, was happy to end the week “with a good feeling” and before travelling to face Switzerland.

He added: “It was not always perfect, but I know that what we worked in two days (this week) happened many times today on the pitch. That's for me very important. On top of that, we created a lot of chances that we really have to score and maybe have a better feeling after the game. But on the whole, I think we were quite aggressive.”

Billy Gilmour missed an open goal shortly after half-time while Dimitrievski pulled off a number of good saves.

“Off the ball, I think we were quite aggressive,” said Pocognoli, who handed a full debut to Stoke City’s Luke Graham in the centre of a three-man defence. “We recover a number of balls that we managed well in some moments of transition.

"We created a big chance for Billy [Gilmour] from this also. So that's a new approach of the game. I think we started the game not that intensely because we didn't manage the ball well. And then for sure you start the game with the feeling that we don't control the ball. After 10 minutes we started to reach Lewis [Ferguson] and Billy [Gilmour] through the lines. And then the game became what we expected.

‘We created chances, we isolated Ben [Gannon-Doak] in the one v one, and we had a lot of pressure. After the first goal I think we need to learn not to drop the intensity. Because after the first goal for 5 minutes I really feel like we dropped the intensity and the focus.

“And we had the same feeling after the second one. So, it's something that we need to fix.”

He agreed Scotland need to be more clinical. “Yes, probably,” he said, while perhaps recalling the missed chances against Slovenia in his first match in charge and which now seem so significant.

‘But I prefer to talk about creating a lot of chances,” he added. “And probably we should keep a clean sheet. So that's really the critical aspect and the demanding aspect. But it's part of the challenge and we are early in the challenge to try to fix this for the future.”

#1834. TMW: Milan one of four teams in the running for want-away Chelsea defender Gusto

AC Milan are interested in signing full-back Malo Gusto from Chelsea, a report claims, but they are not the only Italian club keen.

Milan continue to be linked with potential targets for the flanks, given that they are currently without Samuel Chukwueze and Alexis Saelemaekers due to injury, while Pervis Estupinan and Davide Bartesaghi don’t seem to have fully convinced Ruben Amorim yet.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

According to TMW, Malo Gusto’s name is one to watch. Como are the latest club to enter the running for him, and the right-back is ‘ready to consider a change of scenery’ as early as the upcoming winter transfer window.

The Frenchman is seeking more consistent playing time and is open to leaving London to find more opportunities. Meanwhile, the Blues have not closed the door on the possibility of letting him leave in January either.

Gusto, who joined Chelsea in 2023 after his time at Lyon, has shown significant quality but hasn’t managed to establish himself under Xabi Alonso yet. He hasn’t started any of the last six Premier League games, which speaks volumes.

The opportunity to play more regularly is therefore crucial for the defender, who wants to maintain a central role for the French national team as well. Como, however, will face stiff competition in order to land him.

Atlético Madrid, Milan and RB Leipzig are also pursuing Gusto, all of whom are closely monitoring the situation. Should Chelsea decide to open the door fully, a four-way race to sign him could break out. The Rossoneri boast a good relationship with the London club too, which may help.

#1833. Man United's new boss contenders: Mauricio Pochettino tops the bookies' favourites ahead of Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann on 14-man list of top candidates

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 03:12 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 05:18 EST, 10 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino is the bookies' leading candidate to replace under-fire Michael Carrick as Manchester United head coach should the latter get sacked.

As reported by Daily Mail Sport late on Monday night, Carrick is facing the sack during this November international break as a result of United's disastrous season so far.

Scrutiny on his role has intensified with the Red Devils now in the relegation zone despite salvaging a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino is currently in charge of the US national team, but his contract includes a £7million release clause. However, it is yet to be determined the true value of prising Pochettino out as that figure doesn't include buying out his backroom staff.

It is also believed within Pochettino's deal that there is another clause which would allow him to leave his US role for particular high-profile jobs, such as at Old Trafford.

And Betfair have the Argentine as the favourite to succeed Carrick should he be dismissed within the next fortnight before United travel to bitter rivals Liverpool on November 22.

Mauricio Pochettino is the bookmakers' favourite to become the next Man United head coach

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick is expected to get the sack after a poor start

As of 8.12am on Tuesday morning, they have him at 4/7 with out of work trio Eddie Howe (5/2), Julian Nagelsmann (5/1) and Didier Deschamps (15/2) the next favourites.

Antonio Conte and Aston Villa manager Unai Emery (both 9/1) follow the aforementioned quartet in the odds.

Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler, Kieran McKenna, who worked with Carrick as an assistant manager to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, and ex-England manager Gareth Southgate are all 20/1.

Southgate's successor Thomas Tuchel is 28/1 alongside Diego Simeone, Sebastian Hoeness and Cesc Fabregas.

Nottingham Forest head coach Oliver Glasner is 33/1 too.

As Daily Mail Sport detailed, although it's understood that no final decision has been reached over Carrick's future and insiders say that speculation over his sacking is premature, the expectation within Old Trafford is that a new man will be in charge for the visit to Anfield a week on Sunday.

Carrick replaced Ruben Amorim in mid-January and the former United midfielder was handed a two-year contract in May after guiding United to a third-place finish and qualification for the Champions League, losing just two of his 17 games as head coach.

However, he has only won three of 15 games in all competitions. Breaking it down even further, the 45-year-old has overseen United's worst top-flight start since Sir Alex Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson 40 years ago - with one victory in 10 matches.

#1832. I watched Scotland limp to victory vs North Macedonia and noted astonishing moment and rising star

Sebastian Pocognoli celebrated his first victory at Hampden as Scotland limped past North Macedonia 2-1 in uninspiring fashion last night.

John McGinn’s second half brace proved decisive to secure three valuable Nations League points and keep Scotland's promotion play-off hopes alive ahead of Monday's trip to Switzerland.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The Aston Villa midfielder opened the scoring after the break, only for Elmin Rastoder to equalise almost immediately. McGinn then kept his cool from the penalty spot after 73 minutes following a VAR review to restore Scotland's lead and seal a much-needed victory.

Lewis Anderson watched the action unfold in Mount Florida for The Scotsman and picks out his five main takeaways from the game.

This was far from a classic and a bit of a grind, but securing a first win at Hampden Park was an important milestone for Pocognoli as he continues to find his feet in the Scotland hotseat. Having endured a mixed start to his tenure, the Belgian will have been acutely aware of the importance of delivering a positive result in front of an expectant home support against winless opponents ranked 71st in the world, particularly with Scotland's Nations League promotion play-off ambitions hanging in the balance.

After losing his first two home fixtures in charge, the pressure was on the Belgian to deliver. While the performance was far from convincing, with Scotland squandering several opportunities before allowing a North Macedonia side who had failed to score in their previous eight matches to draw level, McGinn's spot-kick ultimately spared their blushes.

There was little comfort in the manner of the victory, but the three points were invaluable. More importantly, Pocognoli can now look to build on his first Hampden success as Scotland prepare for their decisive trip to St. Gallen, knowing that their hopes of reaching the promotion play-offs remain firmly alive.

The ever-reliable McGinn further cemented his place in Scotland's footballing history with his double, taking his international tally to 24 goals and drawing level with Hughie Gallacher in joint-third place on the country's all-time scoring charts list.

He continues to combine his trademark energy and leadership with an impressive knack for finding the net, and is now firmly in pursuit of the players above him. Only Denis Law and Kenny Dalglish remain out in front with 30 goals apiece, leaving McGinn within touching distance of some of the most illustrious names ever to wear the dark blue jersey.

At 32 and with plenty of international football potentially still to come, the prospect of climbing further up the rankings and surpassing that record is an increasingly realistic one.

Luke Graham enjoyed a hugely encouraging first start in the heart of defence, making a positive impression despite having only two international appearances to his name. This was an ideal opportunity for the Stoke City defender to show that he belongs at international level and can become a regular fixture in Pocognoli's plans.

He looked assured in a back three, showing good positional awareness and a willingness to put his body on the line when North Macedonia threatened. The 22-year-old produced an well-timed sliding challenge early in the second half to snuff out a dangerous attack and also came close to adding a goal at the other end, rising highest to meet a Lewis Ferguson corner but glancing his header narrowly wide. His aerial presence offered an additional threat.

Having made the step up from his brief cameo appearance in last month's victory in Skopje, the former Dundee man has given Pocognoli plenty to consider as he looks to establish himself in the senior set-up.

Scotland remain far from the finished article, but Graham’s performance was an encouraging step in the right direction for a player only at the beginning of his international journey.

Less than a minute into the second half, Napoli’s Billy Gilmour blazed over with the goal gaping from eight yards out from a Che Adams cut-back, summing up Scotland's lack of clinical edge in the final third and creating an instant sense of dread inside the national stadium.

For the Tartan Army, watching that golden, unmissable chance go begging at the same end of Hampden instantly triggered flashbacks to October 11, 2008, drawing comparisons to Chris Iwelumo’s infamous blunder from three yards out in a crucial 2010 World Cup qualifier against Norway.

Both glaring misses occurred in high-stakes fixtures where Scotland were struggling to break down stubborn opposition. Just as Iwelumo's error piled immense pressure on manager George Burley, Gilmour's miss threatened to derail Pocognoli's bid for a desperately needed first home win.

While Iwelumo's miss resulted in a costly 0-0 draw that effectively ruined Scotland's qualification campaign and haunted the striker for years, Gilmour was spared lasting infamy by McGinn, turning his horror moment into a lucky escape.

It was a landmark evening for captain Andy Robertson, who earned his 102nd Scotland cap to draw level with the great Kenny Dalglish as the country's most-capped player.

The Tottenham left-back, who has led his country with distinction for several years, now has the opportunity to move clear of Dalglish's long-standing record when Scotland travel to Switzerland on Monday.

It is a terrific achievement for a player who has become such an influential figure in the national side, both on and off the pitch. Having carried the captain's armband through some of Scotland's most memorable moments in recent years, Robertson now stands on the brink of claiming a place in history all of his own.

A record that has stood for four decades is within touching distance, and few would begrudge him the opportunity to make it his own.

#1830. Hull City an inspiration for decades to come as Sheffield United and co take on Championship's parachute regiment

Along with Ipswich Town and Coventry City, if Hull can stay in the Premier League next season, it will be a shot in the arm for the Championship, just as Leeds United and even more so Sunderland's 2025-26s were.

Because at times in recent years the gap between the top two divisions has felt almost unbridgeable.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Since the introduction of parachute payments in 2006-07, 29 of the 60 relegated teams were promoted back to the Premier League whilst being eligible for them, making them less parachutes, more bungee ropes.

Nevertheless, Coventry and Hull got up last season without them, Hull on the back of a 2024-25 where they only escaped relegation on goal difference, then rebuilt their squad under transfer restrictions which prevented them buying players or even paying loan fees in either window.

As Wilder's Blades try to scramble back this season after a summer of big cutbacks when they lost their parachute payment, it is something to take cheer from.

The veteran manager called the Tigers: "An unbelievable example for the next ten, 15, 20 years in the Championship is Hull City.

"They find themselves in the Premier League which in a way I love because it doesn't go on stats at all, it goes on character, togetherness, spirit.

"It goes on ability and a group that had young players as well as the senior players, and we know quite a lot of them because they played at this club (or Middlesbrough under Wilder) and it just shows you money doesn't buy everything.

"It's about constructing a team that can go nine months and find a way to win. They found a way to win all season, in the (play-off) semi-final and the final.

"They're in the Premier League and they won't give a damn about anyone's opinion about them. Good luck to them."

And despite signing 18 players in the summer, Hull have given themselves a good chance of staying up with a strong start to the campaign built around the core who defeated Boro at Wembley in the play-off final, rather than the shiny new additions presumably intended by the recruitment department to replace them.

Meanwhile, the three teams level on points at the top of the Championship in November's international break – Birmingham City, Boro and Stoke City – have mounted their challenges without parachute money. So too Swansea City and Queens Park Rangers in the play-off places and the Blades two points back.

"Knowing Middlesbrough, the owner (Steve Gibson)'s been incredibly supportive of that football club for a long time," reflected Wilder. "They buy, they sell, they've invested the money from Hayden Hackney and Morgan Rogers.

"There's all different ways but they've been ambitious in their approach.

"Coventry sold well – (Viktor) Gjokeres, Gus (Hamer) and other players.

"It (having a parachute) isn't a guarantee.

"Stoke City have got good owners, a great manager and I'm sure Mark (Robins) will crack it this season. They've not been in the top ten since they've come out of the Premier League (in 2018) and it was a club that under Tony Pulis were top eight for a number of years, accumulating funds.

"It's not always a gimme. That's how difficult the Championship is."

#1829. GdS: Tactics, data and team-mates – the ‘strange case’ of Goncalo Ramos at Milan

The Goncalo Ramos enigma continues to dominate the newspaper columns, as AC Milan try unlock their record signing.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport report, Milan fans hoped they had finally found a top-class striker in Ramos, but his three goals this season are not sufficient compared to expectations and the €70m price tag for which he arrived.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

And yet, the Portuguese centre-forward is still proving to be a factor in the team’s fortunes. The reason for this lies behind statistics that the average fan might ignore, but Ruben Amorim certainly isn’t.

The coach has repeatedly emphasised how Ramos is helping the team, less so the other way around. Looking at the numbers, you can’t argue with him. Gonçalo may not be making it into the top scorers’ table, but his work is well explained by statistics that place him among the top strikers in Serie A.

Which ones? Passes (20.7 per game, first in volume among centre-forwards in the league ahead of Lazio’s Noslin) or touches (2nd), for example. But also the aerial duels won and fouls drawn (19, first among attackers) underscore the importance of his sacrifice too.

There are two considerations that don’t emerge from the statistics, but are equally important. The first concerns the movements that free up or facilitate team-mates, such as the sprint for Milan’s first goal in Genoa.

Alphadjo Cisse found himself all alone in the penalty area thanks to Ramos drawing two of the Rossoblu central defenders towards him, allowing Adrien Rabiot to easily pass to the young Italian who was in lots of space.

The second consideration concerns the pressure and coverage work, which has changed since the start of the season. In the early days, Gonçalo was the first to apply pressure up front, but in doing so, he exposed Modric to too much space to cover in front of or behind him.

Amorim therefore asked the Portuguese to instead harass the opposing playmaker, without attacking the defence in the initial possession. This move allows Luka to run less and think more during the opponent’s possession phase.

We were talking about a Milan side that is helping Ramos less than the centre-forward is helping the team, too. The former Benfica man is 19th in Serie A for shots (26) and 15th for shots on target (10).

While it’s true that the Rossoneri maintain a high standard in terms of the quality of chances created (third in the league for big chances behind Inter and Roma), it’s equally undeniable that they arrive in the final third of the pitch less often than expected. Milan are 12th for touches in the opponent’s penalty area and 12th for shots on target.

In short, Ramos sees the ball mostly where he can’t hurt the goalkeepers. Even if, in relation to goal-scoring chances, he should have scored double in the league: 4.16 xG compared to the just two scored. Still, not enough for a Milan-calibre player.

#1828. Scotland set to face much-changed team as Switzerland boss sets out ‘less serious’ final game plans

Scotland will face a heavily rotated team when they meet Switzerland in their final Nations League group game on Monday, with head coach Murat Yakin admitting he will look to rest several stars.

The 0-0 draw against Slovenia on Friday night confirmed Switzerland’s place as Group B1 winners on 13 points, meaning they’ll be promoted to League A regardless of Monday's result in St Gallen. However, it is a must-win for Scotland if they want to qualify for the promotion playoffs.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Currently third in the group, Sebastien Pocognoli’s team are one point behind Slovenia going into their final group game. To progress to a playoff, they must hope North Macedonia pull off a result against Slovenia in Skopje, while they must also beat Switzerland.

“I was actually a little surprised,” said Yakin after Friday night’s goalless draw. “For them [Slovenia], it was really an all-or-nothing game. But I wasn’t unhappy that they didn’t throw everything forward in the end. I’m relieved that we earned the points we needed. The expectations and pressure were enormous, but we showed a lot of maturity.

“If we convert one of the few chances we had, we win the game. But it's okay like this, too. We put ourselves in a good starting position, and we played it out calmly. It was a mature team performance We knew we were playing against a strong team with a good transition game. It was anything but easy. At times, there were ten players in their own penalty area. The opponent didn't allow much. Slovenia is very tough, well-organized, and sits very deep. We had to be careful there [against counterattacks]. We can be happy and proud.”

However, after securing the result they needed in Maribor, the 52-year-old conceded his side wouldn’t need to take the game as seriously against Scotland, explaining they will use the game as an opportunity to give some fringe squad members a chance to impress ahead of the upcoming European Championship 2028 qualifiers, which begin in March.

Already without experienced captain Granit Xhaka due to a calf injury, the Swiss media believe Borussia Dortmund goalkeeper Gregor Kobel is likely to be rested, with one of Silas Huber, Yvon Mvogo or Marvin Keller deputising. Elsewhere, uncapped squad members such as Samuel Ballet and Roggerio Nyakossi could be given their international debuts when Scotland come to town on Monday.

“We do need the necessary stability and seriousness,” admitted Yakin. “But we’ll definitely make a few changes. There are another three or four guys that I would like to see from the start. Monday is about prestige, points, and putting on a good show for our own fans. There were discussions with the clubs that one or two players would be rested once promotion was secured—but I'm not going to replace the entire team.”

#1826. HMRC chase the estate of late ex-England manager Sven-Goran Eriksson for £3.5MILLION in unpaid tax - because he was 'too busy with his ladies to save'

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 06:19 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 06:25 EST, 10 November 2026

Sven-Goran Eriksson's estate is being chased by HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) for an outstanding £3.5million in tax owed.

It comes as a result of the estate's inheritance following Eriksson's death in August 2024 due to pancreatic cancer.

As reported by Daily Mail Sport last year, the former England manager reportedly had assets worth £4.8m but owed a staggering £7.25m to HMRC alone. He also reportedly had at least £1m outstanding in other debts.

In a bid to help reduce that outstanding debt, his family sold his old mansion called Bjorkefors last year - albeit at a substantial loss.

Eriksson is survived by his son Johan, 47, and daughter Lina, 39 - from his first marriage to Ann-Christine Pettersson - as well as partner Yaniseth Alcides. During his time as England manager he had a high-profile relationship with Nancy Dell'Olio.

Speaking to The Sun, Eriksson's lawyer Anders Runebjer has revealed that the estate has no money left to settle the debt - aside from £300,000 in a UK bank and £1m in a Cayman Islands tax haven. He also stated his focus is now to salvage any money for Eriksson's two children after the ex-Three Lions boss had spent his finances around football and women.

Ex-England manager Sven-Goran Eriksson's estate is being chased for £3.5million by HMRC

In August 2024, he passed away at the age of 76 following a battle with pancreatic cancer

The Swede is survived by his two children Johan, 47, and daughter Lina, 39

'Sven earned millions but was always too busy with his football and his ladies to manage money very well,' said Runebjer.

'I told the HMRC I'm not able to get the money in the Cayman Islands or his UK bank and said they're welcome to seize it.

'They replied that they couldn't do that so I told them there was nothing else left - so they won't get paid.

'Sven was regularly sent bills by the British taxman and paid promptly but they changed the rules and now say he still owes £3.5m plus interest after he passed away.

'They're welcome to take whatever they can get but I'm not giving them anything.

'My priority is trying to get whatever money I can that he left for his children - not the British taxman.'

As aforementioned, Eriksson's estate sold his seven-bed house in Torsby, in his native Sweden - located on the banks of Lake Fryken - but at a reduced price.

According to The Sun, the property was on the market for £2m but his family had to lower the price by £400,000 to attract any prospective buyers.

And they went on to add that an anonymous e-commerce businesswoman has now bought it for an undisclosed sum of at least £1.3m - meaning a potential £700,000 loss on market value alone. However, the loss is greater as Eriksson bought the place in 2002 for £4.5m - meaning the true value lost is around £3m.

Last year, Eriksson's former home in Sweden was sold as his family look to reduce debt

Eriksson lived in the property with his partner Yaniseth Alcides until his death

During his time as England boss, he was in a high-profile relationship with Nancy Dell'Olio

Selling the property was the latest thing Eriksson's family have done in a bid to ease the financial burden they have taken on since his death.

In March 2025, they were forced to auction off his memorabilia - such as a lunch invitation from the late Queen.

Also up for auction was his Armani suit from a 2006 World Cup match with his hand-written team notes still in the pocket.

The 349 items reported to have gone under the hammer for a combined total of £140,000 also include his BBC Coach of the Year trophy in 2001 and a Premier League Manager of the Month award from his time as Manchester City boss.

An Ivory Coast top signed with a special message by former forward Didier Drogba from Eriksson's time as national coach in 2010 was sold as well.

Eriksson was estimated to have received around £7m in pay-offs alone from England, Manchester City and Mexico during his managerial career.

The Swede, who managed England between 2001 and 2006, previously described himself as being 'stupid' with his money.

In one of his last ever interviews, he told The Guardian: 'I was never interested in money - I never took care of it and trusted people to do that for me. I was stupid not to control where the money went. I realised that when I didn't have any more cash!

'I still don't know what I have in the bank.'

#1825. Harrogate Town 4 Altrincham 0: Hosts make use of numerical advantage after Leeds United youngster sent off

Harrogate Town returned to winning ways as they secured an emphatic 4-0 victory over Altrincham in the National League.

Simon Weaver’s men had failed to win any of their previous three games across all competitions, but were thoroughly deserving of three points at the Marcy Fitness Stadium.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Altrincham lost on-loan Leeds United prospect Reuben Lopata-White to a red card after just 13 minutes and the numerical disadvantage helped Harrogate spend the bulk of the afternoon in the driving seat.

Will McGowan opened the scoring early in the second half and the lead was doubled by Morgan Williams just 10 minutes later. Michael Craig weighed in late on, smashing home a thunderous effort, before Rohan Vaughan weighed in to cap an excellent afternoon for the North Yorkshire outfit.

There was little to warm the cockles early on, as both sides took time defrosting on a crisp and biting November afternoon. Each enjoyed spells of posession but little was done with it and wing-backs remained tethered in their own halfs.

Harrogate frontman Shawn McCoulsky prompted the first ripple of applause by getting on the wrong side of Altrincham defender Jake Cooper. While he could not test Harry Isted between the Robins sticks, he did manage to win a corner.

Lewis Cass was left in a heap on the ground in the aftermath of the resulting delivery, but calls for a penalty fell on deaf ears.

The referee did react when Lopata-White - a young defender on loan at Altrincham from Leeds - lunged recklessly at Ellis Taylor. There was barely any hesitation from the official, who was quick to produce a red card.

Altrincham retreated deeper after going a man down and Harrogate seized the initiative, taking control of the affair. Clear-cut chances were initially at a premium but Lewis Cass came within a whisker of getting a boot on the end of an inviting Taylor cross from the left.

Little was being created for McCoulsky, although the forward did direct a header towards goal after rising to meet a Williams free-kick. Unfortunately for the hosts, it lacked power and was held with ease by Isted.

Taylor was proving increasingly problematic for the visitors, who struggled to stem the flow of attacks down the left flank as the first half progressed. He cut in side from the wing and forced Isted down to his right-hand side with a low drive to the near post.

Barely a minute later he reverted to being a provider and picked out Josh Hmami with a clever pass. The playmaker sent a low shot towards goal and saw it deflected just before it could test Isted.

Harrogate continued applying pressure into the dying embers of the first half and their final chance fell to Grant Horton, who met a delivery hung up at the back post but could only head into the side-netting.

A slick corner routine straight from the training ground opened Altrincham up within minutes of the restart but as stars aligned for McGowan, he lost his footing.

Craig had more luck when he pulled the trigger from distance, stinging the palms of Isted with a well-struck effort. Archie Baptistie followed suit with a long-range effort of his own, yet Isted was also equal to that.

Altrincham’s resolve was eventually cracked by McGowan, who swept home a left-footed shot after Taylor picked him out from the left.

Harrogate’s opener did not appear to have whet their appetite for goals, as the Sulphurites remained in the ascendency. McGowan jinked into space inside the box after being fed by Hmami, but was leaning back as he curled towards the top corner and found the wrong side of the crossbar.

Taylor, meanwhile, was evidently enjoying himself down the left-hand side. The former England youth international danced his way in from the left and saw a thunderous effort flash just over.

Altrincham had been offering little sign of life, yet Lucas Weaver had hearts in mouths when he drew an excellent save from Luke Hutchinson on the counter-attack. However, it was not to be the beginning of a Robins revival.

Williams sent a rasping shot in from distance and Isted was rendered helpless as it flew beyond him, doubling the home lead.

The frequency of attacks slowed somewhat in the closing stages of the first half but Harrogate’s grip on the game never loosened.

Altrincham simply could not move from first gear and eventually conceded a third when Craig hammered home the final goal of the afternoon.

Goal number four arrived in stoppage time, when substitute Vaughan rifled home a shot Isted was never going to get near.

Massimiliano Allegri’s team is going through a tough time, and the former Manchester United player himself has had some tough nights. As La Repubblica (via Calciomercato.com) report, Napoli fans are beginning to worry about where things are heading.

The 29-year-old McTominay is at a turning point in his career, one which has been revitalised since his arrival at Napoli and the Scudetto won under Antonio Conte. His current contract with the Neapolitans expires in 2028, but negotiations for a renewal have stalled.

Fabrizio Romano reported that Napoli remain confident in the possibility of reaching an agreement over an extension, but the uncertainty currently surrounding the project, the bad results and doubts about the club’s future are forcing him to evaluate.

La Repubblica add that the discussions have even stalled after positive steps were taken in September. McTominay and his representatives want to better understand the Azzurri’s vision moving forward before finalising a new agreement.

Sky Switzerland journalist Sacho Tavolieri reported that the former Manchester United man’s agent has already held discussions with several English clubs. Napoli have not completely ruled out a possible sale, and the figure would be €25-30m.

His contract is currently worth €4.5m net per season. Napoli would like to extend it until 2030 with a salary increase, but they are unwilling to accept the Scotsman’s demands, who has requested around €7-8m net per season.

According to La Repubblica, at the end of the season McTominay and Napoli will sit down to discuss the terms of the new contract, once the club’s plans are clearer. Several clubs are interested though and are watching closely.

Aston Villa and Manchester United enquired in the summer. In the coming weeks, Real Madrid and AC Milan will also be keeping a close eye on the developments surrounding McTominay.

The Rossoneri are currently well-stocked in midfield with Luka Modric, Adrien Rabiot, Yunus Musah, Ardon Jashari plus options like Ruben Loftus-Cheek and the young Christian Comotto. However, with Amorim at the helm, the prospect of profound change is never far away.

#1822. Hibs struggler’s difficult start addressed as major doubts cast on wisdom of Easter Road transfer

Hibs striker Nathan Lowe’s has been told his early-season struggles at the club evidence the gulf in quality between the Scottish Premiership and the English second tier.

Lowe, 21, joined the club on a season-long loan from Stoke City in the summer, but has struggled to make an impact at Easter Road, scoring just twice in all competitions. Mirroring his difficult loan spells at Wycombe Wanderers and Stockport County last season, sections of the Hibs support are far from convinced by the imposing forward.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

However, former Stoke and Reading striker Dave Kitson believes his difficulties in the capital are in part due to a major difference in style and standard with the EFL Championship, with the 46-year-old questioning whether Lowe’s decision to move to Hibs was a wise one.

“Going up to Scotland was never going to be easy [for Lowe],” said Kitson. “It's two completely different styles of football. Scottish football to English Championship football is night and day. The Championship at the moment is unbelievably competitive. Virtually the whole league has been in the Premier League at some point and come down.

“Twenty years ago, paying £3 million for a striker was a lot. Now £30 million doesn't make anyone bat an eyelid. It's so competitive, which is why culture can be a real difference maker. You can't turn up anywhere, like away at Millwall, and just assume you're going to win. Any team can beat anyone on their day. It's so much harder than it used to be.”

The 21-year-old scored 18 goals in the 2024/25 season for EFL League Two club Walsall, and declared he intended to end the season as the league’s top scorer, saying: “I am by no means am I the finished article and I won't be at the end of this loan. But every season I go into, my aim is to be the top goalscorer in the league. Hopefully I can add to my tally significantly here.”

However, Lowe has scored just one league goal for Hibs this season, and his progress has now been stalled further due to injury. He hasn’t played for the club since the 1-0 defeat to Dundee United on October 10 because of a stress fracture.

Head coach Marink Reedijk revealed earlier this week that he expects to be without his services for an indefinite period and, with his loan spell not going to plan so far, former Stoke favourite Kitson believes he will be experiencing a dose of reality after his ambitious pre-season claims.

“Signing for Celtic or Rangers wasn't really an option for me,” Kitson told Lyllo Casino. “But thinking back, when you look at Celtic and Rangers back then, they had players like Henrik Larsson and Chris Sutton and before that Brian Laudrup, and Paul Gascoigne. That was proper quality. It's hard for them up there now because there isn't Premier League money. It's a tough league to go and prove yourself, especially if you're a young kid going on loan thinking you're going to rip up trees. That path is really difficult to tread these days.”

#1821. Harrogate Town player ratings: Three 8/10s and a standout 9/10 in National League win over Altrincham

Harrogate Town cruised to a 4-0 victory over Altrincham in a meeting of National League promotion hopefuls.

The hosts spent the bulk of the afternoon with a numerical advantage, as the visitors lost on-loan Leeds United defender Reuben Lopata-White to a red card after 13 minutes.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Simon Weaver’s men had to wait until the second half to break the deadlock, but the floodgates opened and Will McGowan, Morgan Williams, Michael Craig and Rohan Vaughan all found the target.

Here are The Yorkshire Post’s ratings from the Marcy Fitness Stadium.

Luke Hutchinson - Had little to do as Harrogate spent the afternoon in control, but did dig the Sulphurites out of trouble with a superb save to deny Lucas Weaver. 7

Sam Dreyer - Recovered well from being spun early on and looked assured. 7

Archie Baptiste - Strong in duels and distributed well from the back. 7

Grant Horton - Won his battles and was an aerial threat in the opposition box. 7

Lewis Cass - Did not look particularly natural performing wing-back duties but was tidy enough on the right flank. 7

Morgan Williams - Capped a strong display with a stunning goal to double the Harrogate lead. 8

Michael Craig - Industrious in the middle of the park - and smashed home the third goal of the afternoon. 8

Ellis Taylor - Tormented Altrincham down the left flank and was comfortably the best player on the pitch. 9

Josh Hmami - Forward-thinking throughout in a bright showing. 7

Will McGowan - Caused plenty of problems for Altrincham and opened the scoring. 8

Shawn McCoulsky - Worked tirelessly and created space for those around him, even if it was not to be his afternoon in front of goal. 7

Rohan Vaughan - Chipped in with Harrogate’s fourth of the afternoon from the bench. 7
